chunks.section: Introduction Optomec is a new powerful tool for additive manufacturing
chunks.text: Introduction Optomec is a new powerful tool for additive manufacturing. It is changing the way materials are printed or adhered to substrates and/or features. The Optomec is an aerosol jet printer and will be my main focus on this project. It has the unique capabilities including a small minimum feature size (10 um) and it can apply a wide range of inks or materials with varying viscosities, for example from 1 cP to 1000 cP. This manual is a documentation that will accompany the user-friendly tutorial videos. These are guidelines that will explain how to use the Optomec effectively and suggest some of the novel things that one can achieve with them for projects in robotics, medical devices, etc. It can support research on a wide range of applications including device with resistors and transistors on flexible electronics. It can even support biological applications, where it can deposit live cells on a wide variety of substrates. It will be widely useful to future researchers in robotics, medical devices, bio-hybrid machines, etc. As an example application depositing PEdot on flexible PDMS substrates for electrostatic adhesion and sensing systems in robotics. Tutorial set up videos are ideal to help new users and non frequent users get up to speed on the tool. Please view all the videos and review this document before attending training. These videos show the step by step process on how to assemble, disassemble the machine, convert CAD models, and design layouts into the software which commands the machine to print. These online videos are available at all times so the user can review as many times as needed and has some prior knowledge before coming to the first training session. This manual will live next to the Optomec and will be used when the user is operating the machine. Generating Print Pattern Files Using VMTools (30 mins) SNF offers computers with VMTools-installed AutoCAD software, and this section intends to provide an overview on how to generate Optomec-compatible print pattern files. A user may refer to VMTools Manual and AutoCAD Manual for details on specific software functions. VM Tools Software Video - https://youtu.be/pj4lFR-dEcE 1. Create print patterns using AutoCAD or other CAD software and save it as a drawing file in .DXF which is the only format supported by VMTools. Since Optomec interprets the CAD data in millimeters, it is recommended to set the AutoCAD dimensions in millimeters when designing the print patterns. 2. Make sure to save any changes to the print pattern .DXF file if you imported it from another CAD software before importing to VMTools. Click on the VMTools icon on the AutoCAD Draw menu to start VMTools. This will open a VMTools utility window with several tabs, including Import, Generic Fill, Images, Export, Tool Config, etc. 3. In the "Import” tab of VMTools utility window, click the "Import Dxf” button to import the currently open .DXF file in AutoCAD. 4. Click the "Generic fill” tab. In the “Generic Fill" tab, the user can specify the filling method (serpentine, perimeter, circle) for various closed shapes. Before proceeding to specifying the filling method, first adjust the items under “General Setting” box which is also presented in the Generic Fill tab. The item “Trace Width" specifies how wide the line of deposited ink will be. The default value is 0.1 mm but it can be adjusted to any value in the

chunks.text: the filling method, first adjust the items under “General Setting” box which is also presented in the Generic Fill tab. The item “Trace Width" specifies how wide the line of deposited ink will be. The default value is 0.1 mm but it can be adjusted to any value in the range of 0.005 ~ 5 mm. The input trace width value is what VMTools and Optomec believe the printed line width will be, and therefore it is not necessarily representative of the actual printed line width. Therefore, this parameter should be adjusted after measurement of printed lines for a specific ink, substrate, and set of printing conditions. If the ink, substrate or printing conditions are changed, the user must print and measure again to determine the actual input trace width. 5. Click the filling method button of choice, and then select the shape entities to be filled in AutoCAD. 6. Click the "Export” tab. In the “Export” tab, the user may define the shutter delay time (msec). By clicking "Export" button, the user can create the toolpath file in .prg format which contains motion and shutter commands for Optomec to print the designed patterns. 7. Open the exported .prg file with notepad. We observed that the exported .prg file presents a syntax error - there is a line comment that is missing its corresponding comment character maker ('!'). To solve this issue, add "!" in front of the line that starts with "REAL CRangle;...” to comment the line and fix the syntax error. Other command lines can also be suppressed by adding “!” in front. 8. If the user is familiar with programming, such as MATLAB, the user may create a custom toolpath generation/optimization code, as there can be unexpected errors with VMTools (e.g. random creation of extra command lines). 9. Save your new .prg onto your USB stick. You are now ready to start setting up the machine! 2. Tool setup (30 mins) 1. Design the print patterns using AutoCAD and VMTools as described in the above Section 1. While print patterns can be edited manually at the printer

Ensure that the settings on the machine (bottom right cabinet under the Optomec) are as desired. a. For fine-feature nozzle printing, the switch must be set to “0.5X head”. For cleaning after, make sure that there is more than 1.5 bottles of isopropyl alcohol and 1/4 of a bottle of Branson cleaning solution underneath the hood in room 155. Depending on the printing specifics, more or less cleaning may be required – this is a general guideline for how much cleaning supplies are needed. 3. If the computer is locked, the password is Optomec1. 3. On the computer desktop, double click the KEWA gadget shortcut to open the KEWA gadget interface. 4. Press "start all” to initialize all KEWA applications. Assembly (Pneumatic Atomizer Mode, Fine Feature Printhead) (20 mins) The Optomec setup begins with assembling the machine. This is an overview of the three important components that will be necessary to run the tool. The atomizer will take your material and atomize it and it will go through the virtual impactor and out the printhead. The exploded views of the three main subassemblies illustrate how individual parts fit together with the O-rings: (1) pneumatic atomizer (Figure 1), (2) virtual impactor (Figure 2), and (3) printhead (Figure 3). Figure 1 shows the pneumatic atomizer assembly, with labels for Thermocouple, Ferrule, Inverted cone, and Ink Jar. The pointed end of the cone faces toward the ferrule. Figure 2 shows the fully assembled Virtual Impactor (Top) and an exploded view (bottom) with O-ring numbering (O-Ring #2-012, O-Ring #2-008, O-Ring #2-016). Figure 3 shows the fully assembled Fine feature nozzle (Top) and an exploded view (bottom) with O-ring numbering (O-Ring #2-008, O-Ring #2-018, O-Ring #2-012, O-Ring #2-008). 4.1 Assembly preparation The following section is about assembly preparation. You will need to do the following steps before setting up the machine. Virtual Impactor - https://youtu.be/mzuX0bs4qNU 3. Using the tube cutter, cut a section of 1/8-in PFA tubing (Swagelok, P/N: PFA-T2-030-100, OD 0.125", Wall 0.030”) into a length sufficient for connecting the printhead with the virtual impactor. Make sure that there is extra length to accommodate the movement of the printhead, but not enough to result in slacking or coiling of the tube, which can cause agglomeration of the ink aerosols inside the tube. It is important that the cut end of the tube is flat and pristine (no angled edge, no cut debris) to avoid gas leakage. (In troubleshooting for leaks, look for tubing that is cut at an angle) 4. Insert first the inverted cone and then the ferrule (Omni-lock inverted cone fitting nut) to the tube such that the pointed end of the cone points toward the ferrule. 5. Assemble the atomizer cap (Figure 4), then pour the ink into the jar (30 mL of ink is the recommended volume, any less volume may adversely affect the aerosolization process), and ensure the tight closure of the jar with the cap. Figure 4 shows an exploded view of the pneumatic atomizer stem (Top), with O-rings #2-008, #2-012, and #2-035, and the atomizer cap (Bottom). 6. Adjust the position of the atomizer stem by loosening the Swagelock fitting around the stem such that the bottom of the atomizer jet is close to the bottom of the jar without touching it. The exact position is not critical. However, it is important to ensure that the atomizer jet hole is approximately 15 mm (= 5/8 in) above the surface of the ink because any deeper immersion of the atomizer jet hole into the ink may result in the interference between the

Be sure to carefully hold onto the stem and cap while inserting stem. 6. Take out the atomizer jet. 7. Screw on the atomizer jet. 8. Lastly screw the jar after you fill it with your desired liquid. 9. Make sure the ink level is 15mm below the small hole on the side of the jet. Connect the tubing and insert the atomizer into the machine. 4.3 Printhead Shutter Subassembly The following section shows how to connect the printhead shutter subassembly. 1. The printhead-shutter subassembly is done by (1) making the B-B connection which is then fixed by part C (mounting the printhead) and (2) making the D-D connection (mounting the shutter using a tiny hex screw). Wide Nozzle Assembly Video - https://youtu.be/uPdCfDcnj4g 2. The printhead-shutter subassembly is then physically mounted to the Optomec system by making the A-A connection which can be done at various angles (i.e. the direction of the nozzle tip with respect to the work stage can be perpendicular or at some angle). 3. Connect part G of the printhead-shutter subassembly to the Optomec system to make electrical connection. The knob E allows the z-axis height adjustment of the shutter with respect to the substrate. While the printhead is connected to the virtual impactor by cutting tubing as described above in the assembly preparation section, a separate tube from the Optomec setup connects to the inlet F of the printhead-shutter subassembly as the sheath gas input. As shown in Figure 4 (on page 23), Optomec offers the alignment camera, which allows the user to view the substrate, as well as the process camera, which allows the user to observe the aerosol stream during printing. They are set up around the work stage on which the substrate is placed. Camera focusing and adjustments can be performed after enabling the tool in Badger, as is described below. Figure 4 (on page 23) illustrates adjusting deposition head (nozzle tip) and shutter height using glass slides, with z-axis adjustment for shutter-printhead subassembly, process camera, and alignment camera. Assembly (Ultrasonic Atomizer Mode, Wide Feature Printhead) (20 mins) The Optomec setup begins with assembling the machine. The exploded views of the three main subassemblies illustrate how individual parts fit together with the O-rings for the wide nozzle printhead. 1. Assemble the wide feature nozzle following same O-ring greasing and checking procedure as described in Section 4. 2. Mount the wide nozzle into the machine as you did with the fine feature nozzle. 3. Add appropriate tubing for the wide nozzle, divert valve output, sheath gas input, and the aerosol input from the atomizer. 4. Turn on and focus your process camera light. 5. Turn on and adjust your alignment camera light. 5.2 UA Max Ultrasonic Atomizer Setup The following instructions are for the setup of the UA Max ultrasonic atomizer. Ultrasonic Atomizer Video -

Ultrasonic Atomizer Video - https://youtu.be/IFBBkoEolWc 1. Make sure all the connections are made and the ultrasonic is fully mounted and set up. The diagram on page 28 shows pump prime and enable switch, UA control cable, atomizer module cable, UA power cables, pump power cable, and UA Max heat exchanger electrical connections. 2. Turn the power on for the machine but do not enable the atomizer power yet. This is to avoid damage until the bath is filled, pump power on, and bath flow has been established. 3. Fill the bath with water and prime the pump. 4. Check the bath level and add water if necessary. 5. Start the water flow. 6. Turn on the chiller unit and set temperature. 7. Carefully slide the vial cap assembly with attached vial out of the atomizer assembly. 8. Unscrew the vial from vial cap assembly. 9. Fill vial with 0.5 to 2.5 mL of atomized material. 10. Replace the vial on the cap assembly top block. 11. Slide the vial cap assembly back onto the atomizer assembly. Check to make sure the gasket for the atomizer gas makes a good seal. Grease the O-ring if necessary. 12. Loosen the knurled nut on the mist tube adapter Swagelok fitting and slide the mist delivery line all the way into the fitting until it bottoms out. Tighten the knurled nut. 13. Make sure the mist tube adapter is mated against the must tube collar. 6. Focus the process and alignment cameras (5 mins) Once the tool has been enabled on Badger, it is possible to focus the process and alignment cameras. To focus both cameras, on the operator panel: 1. Turn on the alignment and process camera lights. 2. Go to KEWA Vision Manager application and select the tab corresponding to the desired camera to focus. A

Check for gas leaks or a clogged nozzle tip (5-30 mins) For optimum performance, all system leaks or clogging must be eliminated before atomization of the ink. This step is of utmost importance – the user should not proceed with atomization if there are any leaks or clogging present in the system, as this could damage components of the tool and/or lead to chemical contamination of tool parts and the user's samples. 1. Monitoring of the sheath gas flow will indicate if there are any leaks or clogging present in the system. 2. Visit Table 1 for the recommended sheath gas flow for optimum performance of the Optomec will depend on the nozzle tip size utilized. 3. Under the pneumatic tab in KEWA Process Control, enter the correct sheath flow value in the Sheath_MFC box. 4. Press enter. 5. The pressure reading will be displayed in the graph in the KEWA Process Control application, as well as next to the Sheath_MFC box. 6. Wait until the pressure stabilizes. 7. A reading below the values displayed in Table 1 indicates that there is a leak in the system. A reading above these values indicates that there is a clog in the system. For troubleshooting of leaks and clogging, go to Sections 8.2 and Section 8.3, respectively. Table 1: Use this table to compare and determine if there are any leaks or clogging in the system. Troubleshooting This section describes common hardware and software issues that we experienced while using the Optomec, as well as strategies for overcoming them. 8.1 Optomec Operating Software (KEWA) Issues Common software issues users have experienced include: 1. Software not starting fully or freezing during operation. 2. Software loading print pattern file but not executing printing procedure. 3. Software not measuring applied sheath, atomizer, or exhaust flow values. Software complications are generally fixed by re-initializing the software or performing a hard reboot of the system. Propose the following procedure: 1. Software permitting, set to zero all the gas flows in the following order: atomizer -> wait 10 s -> exhaust -> wait 60 s -> sheath. 2. Close all applications of KEWA software and re-initialize

chunks.source: Stanford SNF Optomec AJ300 Manual (2018)
chunks.section: the software or performing a hard reboot of the system
chunks.text: the software or performing a hard reboot of the system. Propose the following procedure: 1. Software permitting, set to zero all the gas flows in the following order: atomizer -> wait 10 s -> exhaust -> wait 60 s -> sheath. 2. Close all applications of KEWA software and re-initialize all KEWA software instances. 3. If (2) fails, then turn off the PC, disable the tool using Badger, re-enable the tool, and re-start the KEWA gadget interface. 4. After re-initialization, turn on the sheath flow, exhaust flow and atomizer flow following the procedure stated in Section 7. 5. Run again the homing routine and perform a test print to ensure that the printer is working properly. 8.2 Troubleshooting a Leak During Initialization A reduced sheath flow during tool startup indicates that there is one or multiple components leaking in the system. Leaks can come from various elements, and thorough inspection of assembled components in the tool (as described in Section 4) and connecting elements is imperative. Start by looking for leaks in the most common locations. Leaks most commonly occur at the locations where the tubes connect to the hardware and at the O-rings in the print head, virtual impactor, and atomizer. 1. While troubleshooting leaks, the user should ensure that the sheath gas flow is set to zero before carefully inspecting one item at a time and making any repairs the user deems necessary. 2. Check the connection tubes. 3. Check O-rings, check if they are cracked or not greased well. 4. Check the PFA tubing, despite using freshly cut PFA tubing. Given that some elements of the tool are more prone to produce leaks in the system, we suggest inspection of the tool items in the following order. After performing any repairs in the system, the user should evaluate if the repair eliminated the leak source by applying the recommended sheath gas flow pressure and reading the pressure in the system. Only after the expected pressure is in the range displayed in Table 1 the user can confirm that all leak sources have been eliminated. 1. Connection of

Only after the expected pressure is in the range displayed in Table 1 the user can confirm that all leak sources have been eliminated. 1. Connection of the PFA tube to the printhead: Remove the tube from the printhead and inspect the quality of the cut at the tube's end. If the cut is not flat, use the tube cutter to refine the cut, since any misalignment can produce an improper connection of the tube with the printhead. Attach the tube back to the printhead by pushing the tube all the way into the printhead and screwing the ferrule. To ensure proper connection, attempt to pull the tube from the printhead. If the tube wiggles or moves inside the printhead, the tube was not correctly connected. 2. Connection of the PFA tube to the virtual impactor: Follow the instructions stated in (1) for the connection between the PFA tube and the virtual impactor. 3. Printhead (1st), virtual impactor (2nd), and atomizer (3rd): For each of the components (1-3), remove it from the Optomec and disassemble it following the inverse procedure described in Section 4. Inspect all O-rings for any imperfections and ensure that the installed O-rings are the right size (see printhead: Figure 3, virtual impactor: Figure 2, atomizer: Figure 1). 4. In addition, all installed O-rings must be properly greased. Visually inspect the part every time a sub-component is re-assembled (see Section 4). The user should take special attention to ensure all subcomponents are aligned and that during the re-assembly process no O-rings were damaged. For the re-assembly of the atomizer, ensure that the cap is completely closed. As mentioned in Section 4, the improper fitting between the cap and the jar makes closing and opening the jar a very arduous task that requires quite a lot of physical effort. 5. Replacing the PFA tubing: Cut a new length of tubing and replace the old tubing. Ensure the cuts in both ends of the tube are

chunks.text: between the cap and the jar makes closing and opening the jar a very arduous task that requires quite a lot of physical effort. 5. Replacing the PFA tubing: Cut a new length of tubing and replace the old tubing. Ensure the cuts in both ends of the tube are flat and that the connections of the tube with the printhead and virtual impactor are correct (see 1 and 2). 6. Replacing the nozzle: In a few situations we found that the nozzle had been damaged and was the source of leakage. If troubleshooting all the other components of the Optomec does not fix leaking, then replace the nozzle. Please inform the staff about your issues with the nozzle and label the faulty nozzle. 8.3 Clogged Nozzle Tip An abnormally high pressure on the KEWA Process Control pressure read out window indicates that one or more of the microfluidic components of the Optomec are clogged. Most commonly, clogging will occur at the nozzle tip, but it can also occur at the printhead, virtual impactor, or atomizer. To determine if a component is clogged, remove the part from the Optomec and disassemble following the inverse procedure described in Section 4. Visually inspect the subcomponents of the part in a well-lit area. If the subcomponents present ink material agglomerates, they must be cleaned prior to use. For cleaning clogged components, follow the instructions in Section 11. 8.4 Excessive and Intermittent Jetting of Ink Excessive and intermittent jetting of ink may occur during printing and may worsen over the course of a printing run. This was a common problem when attempting to print PEDOT:PSS. It was observed formation of excessive ink blobs around the nozzle tip which had to be cleaned using a cotton swab between prints to prevent the blob from falling onto the substrate. Additionally, users observed satellite drops which caused their printed patterns to have poor spatial definition. Also observed beads of ink droplets in the tubing that connects the virtual impactor and the printhead (Figure B on page 34), which eventually agglomerated together to form a large ink droplet.

chunks.text: onto the substrate. Additionally, users observed satellite drops which caused their printed patterns to have poor spatial definition. Also observed beads of ink droplets in the tubing that connects the virtual impactor and the printhead (Figure B on page 34), which eventually agglomerated together to form a large ink droplet. This droplet then fell down the tubing, went through the printhead, and finally splashed onto the substrate (Figure C-D on page 34). Such events can be correlated with spikes in the exhaust/sheath/atomizer flow (Figure A on page 34), although the spikes were not periodic. Users have yet to pinpoint the cause of this issue. Possible solutions include: (1) adjusting ink rheology such as diluting the ink to reduce its viscosity, (2) cleaning the virtual impactor and printhead, (3) replacing tubing, and (4) adjusting the "push" which is defined as the difference between the exhaust flow and atomizer flow. The user should take note that the push does not respond immediately, and that there can be residual pressure in the atomizer that exacerbates this delay. Figure A on page 34 shows a screenshot of KEWA Process Control window that shows spikes in the gas flows. Figure B on page 34 shows beads of PEDOT:PSS ink in the tubing that connects the virtual impactor and printhead. Figure C on page 34 shows the large droplet of PEDOT:PSS ink flowing down the tubing and entering the printhead. Figure D on page 34 shows the large droplet of PEDOT:PSS ink splashing onto the substrate. Figure A on page 35 shows PEDOT:PSS printing on paper with good jetting. Figure B on page 35 shows PEDOT:PSS printing on paper with bad and excessive jetting when pressure spikes on the three gas flows were observed. Start Atomizing (2 mins) Once it is confirmed that there is no leaks or clogging, start atomizing the ink. To avoid clogging, always turn on the gas flows in the following order [1]: 1. Sheath flow 2. Atomizer flow 3. Exhaust flow The amount of sheath, atomizer, and exhaust flow required for optimal printing depends on the ink. If these values are not available for the ink to be used, follow the recommended starting parameters in the Optomec manual, which we include in Table 2 for the pneumatic fine feature nozzles. If atomization occurs, the user should see droplets of ink splattering on the wall of the jar, as illustrated in Figure 1 (left on page 8). If no atomization is occurring, slowly increase the atomizer and exhaust gas flow in the proper proportion [1]. Once you see good atomization of the ink, take note of the applied atomizer and exhaust flows. Vary the sheath flow to optimize print quality. You are now ready to print! Enjoy! 10. Disassembly (20 mins) When printing is finished, Optomec parts must be disassembled properly as described below: 1. Turn off the three gas flows in the following order: atomizer -> wait 10 s -> exhaust -> wait 60 s -> sheath. 2. Remove assembled parts from the Optomec: atomizer, virtual impactor, and printhead. a. Any of the following assembly you used: ultrasonic, pneumatic, virtual impactor assembly, wide nozzle and fine feature nozzle. 3. Disassemble the printhead shutter

Dispose of tubing. 5. Clean up the work stage. 11. Cleaning! (4+ hours) Now that you have printed all your parts it is time to clean the machine. Generally, each sonication step per cleaning solution must be repeated several times in newly filled cleaning solution for at least 10 minutes before proceeding to the next sonication step. The order of cleaning solutions is: water, Branson, and isopropyl alcohol. Branson is a specially formulated cleaning solution, and it is effective in removing rust and metal oxides. The Branson solution is prepared by mixing 1 part Branson concentrate to 11 parts water. The minimum cleaning procedure is provided in Table 3, which is suitable for PEDOT:PSS ink, but more thorough cleaning may be required for other ink types. Optomec parts that directly contact the ink are considered to be critical parts and must go through more extensive cleaning. Optomec parts that require thorough cleaning are shown in the image on page 36, numbered 1 through 15. Critical parts are 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12. Plastic parts (ferrules and cones) that can be cleaned together are 16 and 17. Part 18 is a critical part that can not be cleaned with Branson. Part 19 needs to be cleaned first by clean wipes and then sonicated. Part 20 does not need to be cleaned but if it looks dirty wipe it down. Table 3: Minimum cleaning procedure of Optomec parts. The choice of suggested cleaning recipe depends on the part condition and ink. [1] - For non-critical parts: Water (10min x 2 times), Branson (10min x 2 times), Isopropyl alcohol (10min x 2 times). Rinsing with isopropyl alcohol and blow dry with N2 gun. - For critical parts: Water (10min x 3 times), Branson (10min x 3 times), Isopropyl alcohol

Rinsing with isopropyl alcohol and blow dry with N2 gun. Thorough cleaning of Optomec parts after printing is the most crucial procedure of Optomec operation: 1. Disassemble each part (atomizer, virtual impactor, and printhead) into its multiple subcomponents, following the inverse procedure described in the Assembly sections. 2. Transfer disassembled parts to room 155. Place individual subcomponents in a beaker. As a general rule, each subcomponent should be placed in an individual beaker - exceptions are some non-critical parts, such as ferrules and cones, if there is not enough space available in the sonicator to place all subcomponents in separate beakers. 3. Fill beakers with cleaning solution and sonicate for 10 to 15 minutes. Ice cubes should be added to the sonication water bath to prevent overheating. 4. Dispose of cleaning solution in the disposal counter in the fume hood and refill beakers with new cleaning solution. Repeat sonication for 10 to 15 minutes. Repeat this step as many times as necessary according to Table 3 - the specific cleaning solution as well as the number of times this step must be repeated will depend on the user's ink. 5. Leave the parts to dry in the fume hood for 15 minutes then put them away in the Optomec drawers. References: 1. Any changes to this document, however minor, must be submitted for approval by the PI, the college's safety liaison, and EHSS. Overview Setup and initialization of Optomec Aerosol Jet Printer Scope This SOP is intended to be a quick reference guide for assembly and setup of the Aerosol Jet Printer. More detailed instructions can be found in the Optomec AJ 200 Users Guide. Potential Hazards Chemical, Thermal, Mechanical, Radiation, Hydraulic, Pneumatic, Electrical, Fire, Slip/Trip, Fall, Biological, Other. Hazard Specifics: X, Y, Z, movement of stage/print head. Stage heater. Pressurized lines with ink materials. Machine lid. Engineering Controls (EC) Other Local Exhaust, Shielding. EC Specifics: Machine shielding to prevent access during movement and pressurization. Training Requirements – except for classroom lab safety, must be completed prior to performing the procedure Classroom Laboratory Safety Awareness, Lab/Work Group Specific Training (specify): printable ink safety training, Other (specify): waste management. Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) Safety glasses, Lab coat, Gloves. PPE Description: Nitrile gloves, safety glasses, lab coats all provided in eng106. Equipment, Materials, Supplies, & Facility Requirements Optomec AJP200, printable inks, lab wipes, Apiezon grease, compressed air, N2, chiller/H2O circulation system. Handling, Work Area & Storage Requirements Clean workspace, ink cartridges are to be filled in an approved lab space hood, ink materials are to be stored in an approved lab storage space. Emergency Response Equipment & Supplies Eyewash, Fire extinguisher, First aid kit, Spill kit, Safety shower, Fire blanket. Description: Eyewash, safety shower, fire extinguisher, and first aid kit available in ENG106. Spill kit available in eng107. Decontamination & Waste Disposal Solvent trash available in eng106. Spill Response Follow IML SOP guidelines. Notify IML staff. Additional Safety Information Manufacturer Health and safety guidelines document available on printer PC. References Optomec AJP 200 Operators Manual. Procedure STEPS 1.0 Print Head Assembly Potential Hazards: Pinch points. EC, Haz. Mitigation Device, PPE: Always wear gloves and safety glasses. 1.1. Procedure STEPS 1.0 Print Head Assembly Potential Hazards: Pinch points. EC, Haz. Mitigation Device, PPE: Always wear gloves and safety glasses. 1.1. Before using the AJP, you must first assemble the fine feature print head along with the chosen atomizer. There are two options for atomization: 1. Pneumatic 2. Ultrasonic 1.2 Check o-ring integrity on all o-rings. If any damage or contamination is found, replace o-ring. The print head assembly components include an Outer Shell, Upper Insert, Lower Insert, Nozzle, and Retaining Nut, with O-Rings of sizes #2-008, #2-012, and #2-018. The lower insert collar should be flush with the outer shell when installed correctly. 1.3 Using a small swab put a small amount of Apiezon grease on the o-rings and spread it so the entire o-ring is covered with a thin layer of grease. The o-ring should appear shiny and no visible clumps of grease should remain. 1.4 Insert the upper insert into the outer shell. 1.5 Insert the lower insert into the upper insert and press both down into the outer shell. The collar on the lower insert should be flush with the outer shell when installed properly. 1.6 Handle the nozzle with care as the tip is ceramic which is brittle and chips easily. Select your desired nozzle size. Sizes range from 100-300um, sizes are on the vial labels as well as printed on the nozzle itself. Inspect nozzle tip for damage. Press your nozzle onto the lower insert. 1.7 Screw the retaining nut onto the outer shell. 1.8 With the Fine Feature head assembled, you must attach the ink tubing line. Locate the ink tubing that is labeled for the same ink you plan to print. If there is not a line available, contact IML staff and you will be provided with a new section of tubing. Each ink should have its own properly labeled line. 1.9 Thread the blue omnilok onto the line followed by a ferrule. The taper on the ferrule

Each ink should have its own properly labeled line. 1.9 Thread the blue omnilok onto the line followed by a ferrule. The taper on the ferrule should be towards the blue omnilok. Insert the line into the Fine feature head and screw the omnilock down. Give the tube a test pull to see if you can remove it from the fine feature head. If installed properly you should not be able to pull the line out of the fine feature head. The connection involves an Aerosol tube, Omnilok™ fitting and ferrule, leading to the Deposition Nozzle. The groove in the tube aligns with a flange on the bracket. 1.10 After assembling the print head, determine which ink atomizer you will use. The Ultrasonic Atomizer (UA) works best for materials that have a viscosity in the range of approximately 1 - 5 cP. The Pneumatic Atomizer may be used for inks, pastes, or other materials having a viscosity in the range of approximately 1-1000 cP. Continue on to section 2 if you are using the Ultrasonic atomizer or Section 3 if you are using the pneumatic atomizer. 2.0 Ultrasonic Atomizer Assembly Potential Hazards: Pinch points. EC, Haz. Mitigation Device, PPE: Always wear gloves and safety glasses. 2.1 Ultrasonic Atomizer NOTE: See diagram for parts, inspect the o-rings and gaskets for integrity. Reference the Optomec o-ring guide for o-ring size if they need replacement. 2.2 Insert the tube into the black bracket with a hole in it. The groove in the tube aligns with a flange on the bracket. Connect the other black bracket with the countersunk screw. 2.3 Grease the 2-203 o-ring and slide it up the tube and press it into place in the recess on the bottom of the bracket. 2.4 Press the kalrez gasket into the ink vial holder. Make sure it is fully seated below the threads. 2.5 Insert the adaptor on to the ink tube. 2.6 Slide the fitting onto the opposite

Insert tubing into the ink tube adaptor. 2.10 Tighten down fitting onto the adaptor. Give the tubing a test pull and verify that you can't pull it out. 2.11 Carefully attach the ink vial to the ink vial holder. The ink vials are very fragile as they are thin blown gas. The UA Max assembly includes a Tube, Adapter, Fitting, and uses M4X10 BHCS screws, O-ring M2X8, O-ring #2-203, Kalrez gasket 7004167, and a Blown vial 7004210. 2.12 Check o-ring on the atomizer. There is an O-ring for the atomizer gas connection. If the z-axis is close to the stage and you would like more clearance, jump to sections 4.1, then 4.5, then 4.6, then 4.10, then 4.11, then 7.2. This should move the z-axis up and the stage back and to the right to allow the most clearance for print head installation. 2.13 Place ink vial assembly into the atomizer. Do not press it into place yet as you should be holding the print head with your other hand. This involves the Vial cap assembly. 2.14 During this step, make sure that you do not allow the print nozzle to contact the shutter. You can move the shutter down to allow for a little more clearance with the adjustment knob. If the camera is rotated over and in the way, loosen the securing thumbscrew and rotate the camera 90degs to the right. The print head assembly has a Camera securing thumbscrew and an Adjustment knob. 2.15 Insert the print head into the holder. The port and o-ring are for the sheath gas and should slide into the

The print head assembly has a Camera securing thumbscrew and an Adjustment knob. 2.15 Insert the print head into the holder. The port and o-ring are for the sheath gas and should slide into the opening in the holder. With the print head fully seated, carefully slide the clamp around the print head so it is hooked onto the screws on the mounting bracket. Tighten the thumbscrew to secure the print head into place. The clamp hooks onto screws and is secured by a thumb screw. 2.16 After securing the print head in place using both hands to apply even pressure across the entire ink vial assembly, press it down onto the gas fitting. 3.0 Pneumatic Atomizer Assembly Potential Hazards: Pinch points. EC, Haz. Mitigation Device, PPE: Always wear gloves and safety glasses. NOTE: The Pneumatic atomizer has two parts that need assembly, the virtual impactor and the atomizer itself. 3.1 Virtual Impactor Assembly Virtual impactor - Inspect the o-rings. If one needs replaced, reference the o-ring guide for the correct size. The Virtual Impactor assembly includes Housing, Collector, Jet, Stem, Retaining Nut, and various O-Rings (Size #2-008, #2-012, #2-016). The Atomizer assembly includes Ultra-Torr Nut, Atomizer Cap, Stem, Atomizer Jet, Jar, and O-Rings (Size #2-008, #2-012 (Inside Ultra-Torr Fitting), #2-035). 3.1.a Place the collector into the housing, and then insert the jet. Make sure the mist output on the collector is aligned with the hole on the housing. 3.1.b Attach the jet extension tube to the jet and slide on the jet-securing fitting. The jet-securing fitting should thread into the housing; the extension tube should stick out of the fitting. 3.2 Atomizer Assembly 3.2.a Inspect o-rings and ferrules. Replace as necessary. 3.2.b Insert the stainless tube through the lid of the ink jar making sure the correct fittings and o-rings are in the correct orientation. 3.2.c Attach the atomizer jet to the stainless tube and screw the lid onto the ink jar. Before tightening down the fittings, set the position of the jet high

Before tightening down the fittings, set the position of the jet high enough so the hole in the side of the atomizer will be above the expected ink level but the tip will be in the ink. 3.2.d Once you have your desired position set for the atomizer, slide the o-ring down the tube so the fittings can be secured in place. Make sure that the ferrule and omnilock that are on the temp probe are in good shape. 3.2.e Insert temp probe into the ink jar through the designated hole in the lid. Position the temp probe so that the tip will be in the ink but not interfere with a magnetic stirring rod. The assembly ensures the Mist output of collector aligns with the Hole in atomizer and Hole in housing. 3.3 Connecting The Pneumatic Atomizer 3.3.a The first connection is the virtual impactor to the atomizer via the quick disconnect fitting on the side of the atomizer lid. The second is the ink line from the print head. With an omnilock inserted onto the ink line, insert a ferrule so that the taper is towards the omnilock. 3.3.b Now thread the omnilock into the virtual impactor housing. 3.3.c Move the whole assembly over to the printer and place the atomizer in the correct position. Install the print head as described above in section 2.14. 3.3.f Now make the exhaust connection to the virtual impactor via the quick disconnect fitting on the side of the virtual impactor and tubing labeled exhaust on the printer. The fourth connection is the gas line for the atomizer. It is also a quick disconnect fitting and the line is label atomizer gas. It connects to the stainless tube sticking out of the ink jar. The connections are From atomizer, through the Virtual impactor, To print head, with an Exhaust gas output. 4.0 System Power

The connections are From atomizer, through the Virtual impactor, To print head, with an Exhaust gas output. 4.0 System Power On and Initialization 4.1 Turn on the system power using the System power switch. 4.2 Turn on vacuum pumps. 4.3 Turn on N2. 4.4 Turn on System chiller and check fluid circulation. 4.5 Press the blue button next to the tan box that has the Emergency machine off button. The blue button should light up. 4.6 Double click the KEWA Gadget Icon on the PC desktop. The KEWA Gadget Interface (Aerosol Jet Controls v.2.0.30 P M V D U Start All Save Reset) should popup. 4.7 Click on the [P] for Process Control, on the KEWA Interface. The KEWA Process Control window should popup. 4.8 Referencing the pressure table on page 30 of the user's guide for the fine feature print head. Determine how much sheath gas to flow based on the tip size you are using. Located further down the table, determine the pressure reading feedback that you should be getting, this is based on elevation and tip size. Boise is around 2500ft elevation. Input for Sheath gas flow entry and toggle for gas on/off are available, with Pressure feedback and Gas Flow feedback indicators. 4.9 Enter the correct amount into the sheath gas box and press enter or click on the grey circle to the left. Circle should turn green when gas is flowing. Verify that the correct amount of gas is flowing in the gas flow feedback. Allow pressure to stabilize for ~60secs. Check the pressure feedback and compare it to the values you found in the table. ATTENTION: If the pressure reading is lower than the range, you have a leak in the system and need to recheck your assembly. If the pressure is higher, then there is a clog in the system and you need to check your assembly. If the pressure reading is not

If the pressure is higher, then there is a clog in the system and you need to check your assembly. If the pressure reading is not in the correct range, turn off sheath gas flow by clicking on the green circle on the left side of the sheath MFC row. Wait ~30secs and double check your atomizer and print head assemble. 4.10 After you have achieved the correct pressure range, go back to the KEWA gadget application and click on the [M]. The motion controller window should popup. NOTE: Reference Chapter 4 in the user's manual for further details regarding the Process Control Manager. 4.11 About ~ 15seconds after clicking on the [M], you should get a popup that asks if you want to start the homing process. Verify that the platen/stage is clear and click [YES]. Then the motion manager window should popup. On this page, you can control the stage motion, the z-axis motion, platen vacuum, and shutter. You also use this page to set process speed and load your patterns after you optimized your lines. 4.12 Setting the Z Height. 4.12.a Use the buttons in the upper left corner to jog the platen so it is under the print head. Once the platen is under the print head move the print head down so it is close to the platen or your substrate. Place three microscope slides next to the printing nozzle. Adjust the z height until the nozzle is at the same height as the 3 slides. Now adjust the shutter so that there is a gap between the nozzle and shutter that is the same as a microscope slide. The deposition head is adjusted correctly when the nozzle is at the same height as three stacked slides or a spacer. 4.12.b Shutter height adjustment knob. 4.13 On the KEWA gadget application, click on the [V] for Vision Manager. The vision manager should popup. NOTE: Reference Chapter 5 for further details regarding

The vision manager should popup. NOTE: Reference Chapter 5 for further details regarding the motion manager. 4.14 On this page you can select which camera you are using. By clicking on the [Alignment] or [Process] tabs. You will be using the process camera initially. Since you have already set the correct z height for the nozzle you can focus the process camera at this time. Use the focus knob so that the platen or substrate come into focus with the process camera selected. You will use the alignment knobs once you start depositing ink. The system features a Focus Knob and Alignment knobs. 5.0 Ink Filling and Initial Line Tuning 5.1 Remove the ink vial. 5.1.a Clean your substrate and place it on the platen/stage. The platen vacuum should already be turned on. If your sample/substrate moves around freely then can tape it to the stage/platen. If you tape your sample down you can turn off the vacuum pump labeled platen. 5.1.b If you need a heated platen/stage turn on the platen heater and set the temp. The heater switch is on the control rack next to the system power switch. chunks.text: Aerosol-Jet Printed Fillets for Well-Formed Electrical Connections between Different Leveled Surfaces Abstract: As additive manufacture becomes more prevalent in the fabrication of advanced electronics, there is a need to create well-formed, robust circuitization, and interconnects between components mounted onto different leveled surfaces (DLSs). Here, an algorithm is developed for aerosol-jet printing of fillet structures that enable such a circuitization and hence a smooth electrical transition between the DLSs. The fillets are printed using an ultraviolet-curable polymer ink in the presence of in situ curing. A specific deposition rate is established in order to ensure a precise architecture. Further, a surface smoothing technique is employed to smooth out the stepped surface topology of a fillet resulting from the layer-by-layer printing of in situ cured material. Finally, it is ascertained that the performance of these printed fillets is highly satisfactory by carrying out the resistance measurements of the conducting lines printed over these fillet structures both before and after temperature cycling and establishing the mechanical stability of the fillets by employing an adhesion test. This technology ensures that the fillets not only establish a mechanical integration/attachment of the two DLSs, but more importantly that they also provide a well-formed surface onto which an electrical connection between these two DLSs can be established. 1. Introduction Additive manufacturing (AM) (also known as 3D digital printing technologies or more colloquially as 3D-printing) is a promising manufacturing method, which allows for the design and fabrication of complex structures not otherwise achievable using standard (subtractive) manufacturing methods. Additive manufacturing methods have been utilized extensively in the area of structural prototyping in, for example, the automotive and aviation industries. Further advances in AM are bringing the fabrication of electronics into the realm of 3D printing. Such additive manufacturing methods for the fabrication of electronics are expected to greatly advance the design of both printed hybrid electronics (PHE) and flexible hybrid electronics (FHE), which are predicated on the expectation that advanced electronic circuits will be constructed such that new form factors can be obtained. For the PHE this would be in the form of conformable/embedded electronics, while for FHE

chunks.section: advance the design of both printed hybrid electronics (PHE) and flexible hybrid
chunks.text: advance the design of both printed hybrid electronics (PHE) and flexible hybrid electronics (FHE), which are predicated on the expectation that advanced electronic circuits will be constructed such that new form factors can be obtained. For the PHE this would be in the form of conformable/embedded electronics, while for FHE this would be fully flexible electronics. For example, advanced electronics could provide, for some applications, an alternative to a standard Cu/FR4 flat, rigid printed circuit boards (PCBs) generally found in present-day computers and other electronics devices such that the electronics could be fabricated directly into the part itself. Examples of such advanced electronics are a smart electronic bandage for the health care industry or an impact sensor and/or communication electronics built into the shell of a sports helmet. Such electronics are expected to require the ability to mount and electrically connect components comprised of different materials and thicknesses (i.e., embedded/integrated components rather than surface-mounted components that were attached as the last step in fabrication) during the fabrication of a desired circuit. While the ability to thin the components in order to achieve true flexibility may be needed for FHE, PHE is expected to be able to utilize components of varying thicknesses. However, this will most likely require a robust way of creating a smooth transition onto and off of the embedded components, i.e., to smoothly route electrical interconnects over surfaces with inherent step transitions, that is to say between different leveled surfaces (DLSs), as alluded to in Figure 1. Furthermore, a capability is needed to precondition uneven or rough surfaces to a required smoothness value so that well-formed electrical circuits and interconnects can be deposited. In order to address these essential requirements, in this study we have developed algorithms for designing smooth transitions between surfaces and have developed robust processing methods for the fabrication of these transition ramps that are designed to smoothly connect (both electrically and mechanically) DLSs. Typically, smooth transitions between DLSs (combination of a bare IC chip and a substrate is a typical example of a DLSs system) are achieved by syringe-dispensing an epoxy or underfill type

chunks.section: methods for the fabrication of these transition ramps that are designed to smoot
chunks.text: methods for the fabrication of these transition ramps that are designed to smoothly connect (both electrically and mechanically) DLSs. Typically, smooth transitions between DLSs (combination of a bare IC chip and a substrate is a typical example of a DLSs system) are achieved by syringe-dispensing an epoxy or underfill type material around the edge of a component in a way that is illustrated in Figure 1b. While this may be adequate for large-scale features and low densities of thick interconnects, as is reported by Seifert et al., a more controllable method is expected to be required as feature sizes and thicknesses are reduced and interconnect densities are increased. As advanced circuits become smaller and more complex, a more precise control over the volume of the material deposited and the exact geometry of a printed fillet (the structure used to smooth out the height transitions between surfaces) is needed. Therefore, we have developed an aerosol-jet (AJ) printing method for the precise control of the geometry of a printed fillet for the creation of a smooth structural transition between DLSs. The unique printing algorithm consists of (a) a precise determination and regulation of the deposition rate of a printed polymer ink, which is in situ cured and (b) the employment of a novel smoothing and gap-filling approach by printing the same polymer ink followed, after an appropriate time delay, by a postprinting cure. Most importantly, we establish that our printing strategy ensures continuous 3D printed conductive circuits across DLSs, with the circuits demonstrating robust thermal stability and good adhesion properties. The most important feature of the fillet technology that we have developed is that rather than the fillets being a by-product of the mechanical attachment of an object to a surface, they are a precisely engineered and fabricated structure to support an electrical conductor transitioning between DLSs. Our fillet technology is distinctly different from the fillets present in all the current wire-bonded chip packages used in industries. In these chip packages, the fillets are merely used to mechanically integrate the two DLSs, while the electrical connection between these two surfaces is achieved

chunks.section: electrical conductor transitioning between DLSs
chunks.text: electrical conductor transitioning between DLSs. Our fillet technology is distinctly different from the fillets present in all the current wire-bonded chip packages used in industries. In these chip packages, the fillets are merely used to mechanically integrate the two DLSs, while the electrical connection between these two surfaces is achieved via wire bonding. Our study provides a completely alternative mechanism for electrically connecting DLSs by using fine-pitch printed conductors over microstructured fillets. This approach has important advantages over wire-bonding, such as (a) not requiring the extra space in the z-direction and the longitudinal direction that is required to accommodate the arch of the bond-wire, (b) not requiring clearance between adjacent pads to accommodate the wire-bond tool capillary, (c) eliminating the risk of short-circuits between adjacent conductors, where bond wires have increasing risk of short-circuits as interconnect density increases, (d) reducing the electrical length of interconnect, and (e) limiting and controlling the electrical impedance discontinuity caused by the interconnect. In all, we believe that our proposed fillet technology is a significant advance of the current state-of-the-art in the broad area of fabrication and integration. 2. Modeling of Fillets In much the same way that other 3D printing methods slice up the volume of a structural part so that it can be printed one layer at a time, a surface transition ramp (termed a fillet in this paper) can also be sliced. In general, the slicing is performed perpendicular to the ink stream so that uniform layers can be deposited. Figure 2 illustrates two interesting orientations for which a surface transition ramp might be sliced. The ability to print such surface fillets is dependent on the geometry attainable with a given tool platform. For example, the fillet illustrated in Figure 2a would require a printing system equipped with a vertically mounted (z-axis direction) print-head and only an x-y stage as illustrated in Figure 3a, while the fillet illustrated in Figure 2b would further require either the print-head or the part to be rotated by 45° as illustrated in Figure 3b. Additionally, for the orientation shown in Figure 2b, the part (or print-head)

chunks.text: direction) print-head and only an x-y stage as illustrated in Figure 3a, while the fillet illustrated in Figure 2b would further require either the print-head or the part to be rotated by 45° as illustrated in Figure 3b. Additionally, for the orientation shown in Figure 2b, the part (or print-head) would have to be reoriented from +45° to -45° depending on whether the DLSs is oriented to the right or to the left. Depending on the part and/or the tool platform size, there may not be enough room within the printer to accommodate such an orientation. While the 45° orientation might be more desirable, on a two or three-axis tool platform it could require refixturing the part multiple times to reach all the desired part orientations. In general, however, it would require a five-axis tool platform to implement. While five-axis tool platforms are expected to become more available, currently many printers are not equipped with the ability to easily tilt a part or print-head. Therefore, we will focus on developing methods for printing ramps using tool platforms restricted to motion along only three orthogonal directions. This restriction will require a part orientation as shown in Figure 3a and a slicing geometry as shown in Figure 2a. The width of an ink stream is much narrower than the dimensions of the fillet layers, as illustrated in Figure 2a, so each slice/layer will need to consist of a serpentine fill. If, for the purpose of creating a toolpath, the cross-sectional area of the first single printed line can be modeled using a triangular shape of height (h) and base (2h), then each layer can be segmented into serpentine lines on a pitch (p) equal to the height (h) of the modeled triangle of this first printed line as illustrated in Figure 4. Setting the pitch of the serpentine lines to be equal to the height of this modeled triangle ensures a good overlap between printed lines in a given layer, which can help in the formation of a smooth, continuous layer surface. It should be noted that since the overlap of the

chunks.section: Setting the pitch of the serpentine lines to be equal to the height of this mode
chunks.text: Setting the pitch of the serpentine lines to be equal to the height of this modeled triangle ensures a good overlap between printed lines in a given layer, which can help in the formation of a smooth, continuous layer surface. It should be noted that since the overlap of the printed line segment is related to the serpentine fill in a given layer, area elements after the first line segment are represented by parallelograms of equal area. Further note that the closest approach of the center of the ink stream to the vertical sidewall is equal to one-half of the ink stream width (w). This restriction is to ensure that extra material does not build up on the top surface during printing. This restriction is illustrated in Figure 4 and results in only half the needed material being printed at the sidewall. This deficiency was overcome by adding an extra line at the sidewall for each layer printed with half as much material (by printing at twice the linear print speed, as discussed later). Design requirements related to this restriction will be presented in more detail following the main development of the algorithm for creating a printed fillet. The overall dimensions of a fillet and the dimensions for a single area element (equal in area to the cross-sectional area of a single printed line) are illustrated in Figure 4. The cross-sectional area of the fillet (A) can be expressed as A = H²/2. The volume of the fillet (V) is given as V = Al = (H²/2)l. And the cross-sectional area of a single area element (a) is given as a = h². In the above equations, H is the distance between the DLSs and h is the height of a single area element. Of course, Equations (1)–(3) assume that both the entire fillet as well as the single area element can be modeled as isosceles right triangles. Now, the total number of printed lines (N) needed to create a fillet is simply the number of area elements that are needed to fill the fillet cross sectional area. Therefore N

chunks.text: both the entire fillet as well as the single area element can be modeled as isosceles right triangles. Now, the total number of printed lines (N) needed to create a fillet is simply the number of area elements that are needed to fill the fillet cross sectional area. Therefore N = A/a = H²/(2h²). Furthermore, the number of total slices/layers (n) needed to create the fillet is by definition n = H/h. For a fillet of length (l), the total length (L) of all the printed lines added together is given as L = Nl = (H²/2h²)l. As with the printing of any layer or feature(s), the total print time (T) can be obtained as the ratio of the total volume to be printed (V) to the deposition rate (R) of material volume per unit time or the ratio of the total length to be printed (L) to linear print speed (s). So, T = L/s = V/R. This can be rewritten as R/S = V/L = Al/Nl = a. Employing these equations to design and then print a fillet will result in a structure similar to that illustrated in Figure 4. Given that the ink stream cannot be centered at the vertical transition between DLSs, only half the desired material will be deposited at the sidewall, thus creating a "gap." To account for this "gap," an extra line of material at the sidewall can be printed at a speed of 2s after the completion of the printing of each layer. If this extra material has a low-enough viscosity and is not immediately cured, this deposited material, due to the favorable self-wettability and the resulting surface tension forces at the sidewall, will be able to flow into the gap and fill it. In reality, not all the extra uncured material flows into the gap, but rather some sticks to the previously printed line. Therefore, decreasing the amount of material printed in the first line by using a print speed of 1.5s rather than s (a faster print speed deposits less material) and increasing the amount of material printed in the

chunks.text: flows into the gap, but rather some sticks to the previously printed line. Therefore, decreasing the amount of material printed in the first line by using a print speed of 1.5s rather than s (a faster print speed deposits less material) and increasing the amount of material printed in the extra line by using a print speed of 1.5s rather than 2s (a slower print speed deposits more material) is desirable. Additionally, once a fillet has been fully printed, a seam can exist between the top surface of the DLSs and the top of the fillet; therefore, it is good practice to also print an extra line to seal this seam and provide a smooth transition at the top of the fillet. Furthermore, "bulb" formations, as discussed by others, may happen at the termination of a printed feature due to build plate decelerations and time delays related to shutter opening and closing. In order to minimize effects related to such "bulb" formation, the ends of a fillet were tapered inward as illustrated in the inset of Figure 4. An additional issue related to the AJ printing of a fillet is expected to be related to the viscosity of the ink. In order to be able to aerosolize a material for printing, the viscosity will have to be in a range where the ink, once printed onto a surface, will flow and therefore not retain a desired shape. For a UV-curable polymer ink, however, this can be overcome by curing the material in situ. However, such in situ processing tends to produce topologies that result in nonflat surfaces because the material is not allowed to flow enough to self-level. In the printing of fillets, this effect will tend to produce a stair-step type structure as one layer is printed on top of another, as illustrated in the inset of Figure 4 and in Figure 5. The resulting fillet surface can be smoothed by printing an additional layer of material that is allowed to flow and self-level prior to curing. This can be done by individually reprinting each of the serpentine lines

The resulting fillet surface can be smoothed by printing an additional layer of material that is allowed to flow and self-level prior to curing. This can be done by individually reprinting each of the serpentine lines of the first layer of the fillet with an appropriate time delay between printing and curing such that each printed line is allowed to flow/relax enough to smooth out the initial topology. This concept of surface smoothing is a general concept that can be applied to any surface containing a measurable topology. In a general sense, the topology of a surface can be mapped and a toolpath that is designed to deposit a specific amount of material at locations that are deficient of material can be generated. Then the deposited material can be given an appropriate amount of time to relax and flow into a smooth surface before curing the material. Based on the above equations and discussion, any fillet of height H and length l can be designed by the following these steps: 1. Choose the height (h) of a single printed line such that (n) is an integer. 2. Create n layers, where the i-th layer has a width ωᵢ = H + (1 – i)h and length (l), then set a serpentine fill of pitch (p) equal to (h) for each layer. Finally, print and in situ cure the first line in each layer at (1.5s) and the rest of the lines at (s). 3. For each layer, add one extra line centered at a distance of w/2 from the edge of the sidewall to be printed (uncured) at a print speed of (1.5s). 4. Establish a surface smoothing layer—recreate the first layer where alternating between the printing and curing for each line in the serpentine fill will be employed. 5. Add one extra line centered at the edge of the top surface of the DLSs to seal the seam between the fillet and top surface. 6. Set the deposition rate and the print speed of the

chunks.text: printing and curing for each line in the serpentine fill will be employed. 5. Add one extra line centered at the edge of the top surface of the DLSs to seal the seam between the fillet and top surface. 6. Set the deposition rate and the print speed of the printer based on their relationship defined in Equation (8). 3. Aerosol-Jet Printing of Fillets Using the experimental procedures presented above, two separate DLSs samples were fabricated with H = 1 mm and H = 375 µm. For these samples, the deposition rate (R) is a crucial factor in dictating the quality of printing. For example, for the H = 1 mm fillet, a ΔR = 10% would translate into a fillet height change of ≈ΔH = 50 µm. In order to evaluate the significance of a varying deposition rate on the structure of the printed fillets, H = 1 mm fillets were printed at R = 0.0055, 0.0059, and 0.0063 mm³ s⁻¹. Figure 6a shows a fillet printed at R = 0.0055 mm³ s⁻¹, confirming that insufficient material was deposited resulting in a fillet that did not reached the top DLS surface. The existence of a sharp edge coming off the top surface is observed in the confocal microscopy images in Figure 6b. A fillet fabricated at R = 0.0059 mm³ s⁻¹ is shown in Figure 6c. For this case, although the seam at the edge is evident, the height of the fillet is at the same level as the top DLS surface, as witnessed from the confocal microscopy images in Figure 6d. Figure 6e,f shows the optical and confocal images of a fillet printed at R = 0.0063 mm³ s⁻¹ resulting in a structure that is higher than the corresponding top surface of the DLSs. Conclusion In order to establish well-formed, robust electric circuitization and interconnects between components mounted onto DLSs, we have developed and presented an algorithm for the aerosol-jet printing of fillets using tool platforms employing only three orthogonal axes of motion. The importance of controlled and stable deposition rates was demonstrated along with the need for in situ curing of the printed polymer materials in order to fabricate a desired structure. An additional surface modification was discussed for smoothing the topology of these printed structures, which is based on allowing surface printed material to flow/self-level for an appropriate amount of time before curing. Experimental Section Two separate DLSs samples were established. The first sample consisted of two, 1 mm thick glass slides glued together and the second of a 375 µm thick, 1 cm sq blank Si chip glued onto an FR4 substrate. For these two fillet examples, the above described algorithm will generate the fillet printing parameters that are listed in Table 1. Flexible and Printed Electronics PAPER Principles of aerosol jet printing Ethan B Secor Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM 87185, United States of America E-mail: ebsecor@sandia.gov Keywords: printed electronics, nanomaterial inks, direct-write printing, fluid mechanics, aerosol physics Supplementary material for this article is available online Abstract Aerosol jet printing (AJP) has emerged as a promising method for microscale digital additive manufacturing using functional nanomaterial inks. While compelling capabilities have been demonstrated in the research community in recent years, the development and refinement of inks and process parameters largely follows empirical observations, with an extensive phase space over which to optimize. While this has led to general qualitative guidelines and ink- and machine-specific correlations, a more fundamental understanding based on principles of aerosol physics and fluid mechanics is lacking. This contrasts with more mature printing technologies, for which foundational physical principles have been rigorously examined. Presented here is a broad framework for describing the AJP process. Simple analytical models are employed to ensure generality and accessibility of the results, while experimental validation using a silver nanoparticle ink supports the physical relevance of the approach. This basic understanding enables a description of process limitations grounded in fundamental principles, as well as guidelines for improved printer design, ink formulation, and print parameter optimization. chunks.text: aerosol gas flow ratio Printed electronics is an emerging application area for functional nanomaterials, with widespread utility spanning flexible circuits and displays, electronics packaging, and environmental and biomedical sensing. In a typical process flow, liquid inks containing dispersed nanomaterials are deposited with high pre-cision using a suite of printing methods, such as inkjet, aerosol jet, gravure, flexographic, and screen printing. While many of these techniques have an exten-ded history, aerosol jet printing (AJP) is a relatively recent addition to the printing toolbox. In AJP, a functional ink is aerosolized and delivered to the sub-strate by a carrier gas, achieving resolution as fine as 10 µm. Due to its non-contact, line-of-sight, and digi-tal nature, AJP offers advantages complementary to many traditional methods. AJP has been employed in academic research for slightly over a decade in a wide variety of demonstrations. Some of the first examples of use include transistors and more complex circuits, and it continues to be widely used in this field today. More recently, microscale additive man-ufacturing was demonstrated by AJP, in which three-dimensional scaffold structures with hierarchical por-osity were demonstrated using a silver nanoparticle ink. AJP has been used in applied areas of research, for example metallization of photovoltaics and circuit boards, as well as newer fields such as perovskite and kesterite solar cells and terahertz metamaterials. A hallmark of AJP, and a fea-ture underlying its expanding use, is its versatility and compatibility with a broad range of materials, from organic semiconductors and carbon nanomaterials to functional ceramics and composites. Despite its prevalent use in academic research, AJP has several drawbacks well-known to day-to-day users. Although the process is tolerant of a wide range of inks, determining optimal print parameters is often a sensitive process. Related to this, consistency and reproducibility are challenging to achieve, and can require extreme measures such as frequent replace-ment of ink, hindering translation to a production environment. Finally, optimal printing parameters for a given ink do not in general translate to new materials, demanding an extensive, empirical optimization over a broad phase space for each additional ink or mat-erial. These problems stem, in

Finally, optimal printing parameters for a given ink do not in general translate to new materials, demanding an extensive, empirical optimization over a broad phase space for each additional ink or mat-erial. These problems stem, in large part, from a lim-ited fundamental understanding of the process. While mature methods such as inkjet and gravure printing have been widely studied for decades, and have a body of knowledge describing the underlying physical mechanisms, the nascent technique of AJP cannot leverage such a strong theoretical foundation. In the rare attempts to address this need, analyses have largely focused on a single aspect of the overall process. This work is an effort to remedy that shortcoming. Basic models for the discrete physical processes involved in AJP are assembled to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the overall method. Simple, analytical models are deliberately chosen over more involved numerical simulations to maintain generality and accessibility, and to more effectively intuit and conceptualize the underlying physics. Despite the rudimentary nature of the mod-els, some of which represent textbook scenarios in aerosol physics and fluid mechanics, the resulting description is well validated by experiments. This pro-vides a valuable benchmark for experimental results, to identify and correct inefficiencies in the ink chem-istry and process conditions. Moreover, this basic understanding of the principles of AJP enables an exploration of process limitations grounded in funda-mental fluid mechanics, providing guidelines for improved printer design, ink formulation, and print parameter optimization. Methods Experimental testing was carried out using a Nanojet printer with a silver nanoparticle ink. For most experiments, the base ink was obtained from UTDots (UTDots Ag40X-AJ) and mixed with xylenes and tetralin at 2:7:1 v/v ink/xylenes/tetralin. For figure 3(b), a wet ink (2:4:4 v/v ink/xylenes/tetralin) was used to reduce impaction and sheath gas-induced drying effects. When not in use, the inks were stored in a cool environment at 0 °C-10 °C. During printing, the ink cartridge was held at 17 °C, the substrate was held at 40 °C-80 °C, and the atomizer power was controlled

During printing, the ink cartridge was held at 17 °C, the substrate was held at 40 °C-80 °C, and the atomizer power was controlled with a potentiometer set at ~27 V. Fisnar deposition tips were used for printing, with nozzle diameters of 160, 233, and 335 µm. Glass slides were used as a substrate, and printed samples were thermally annealed at 200 °C following printing. All mathematical models were implemented using MATLAB software. Results and discussion AJP overview A general schematic of AJP, broken down into its component physical processes, is shown in figure 1(a). Ultrasonic atomization is used to generate droplets of the active ink. Due to the micron-scale size of the droplets, solvent evaporation occurs rapidly, resulting in a reduction in droplet size. A carrier gas, referred to herein as the aerosol gas, transports the droplets to the deposition head. During transit, two mechanisms can lead to losses—gravitational settling and impingement on tube walls by diffusion. In the deposition head, a sheath gas surrounds the aerosol gas, collimating the beam. As they pass through a deposition nozzle, droplets can be diverted from their flow stream due to inertial effects in the narrow, converging nozzle, leading to aerodynamic focusing. Finally, the droplets are directed towards the substrate in an impinging jet. Each of these processes can be described with knowl-edge of the system geometry and the key process parameters—the aerosol and sheath gas flow rates, the deposition nozzle size, and the aerosol droplet size. Additional parameters such as atomizer power, print speed, and ink and substrate temperatures are con-trolled in operation, but have peripheral effects around the core processes. Atomizer power and ink temper-ature (which affects viscosity) affect the inputs to the process, namely droplet size distribution and aerosol density. While atomizer power and ink temperature are not explicitly treated here, the droplet size distribu-tion and aerosol density are considered. In addition, print speed affects the print thickness and the substrate temperature affects

While atomizer power and ink temperature are not explicitly treated here, the droplet size distribu-tion and aerosol density are considered. In addition, print speed affects the print thickness and the substrate temperature affects drying following deposition, which can affect resolution in certain cases, film uniformity, and morphology. While important for the process, deviations due to these effects are largely ink-specific. Therefore, this work will address these factors as they fold in around the core AJP process, without an explicit treatment. There are two primary commercial systems for AJP. The most prevalent one, having been around for over a decade, is manufactured by Optomec. The experimental portion of this work employs an alternative design from Integrated Deposition Solu-tions, Inc. known as the Nanojet (figure 1(b)). Due to its simple design, this machine is amenable to the broad study of process parameters included here. While constructed differently, these printers operate on the same general mechanism described above, and can provide an informative contrast when assessing the principles of the process. Therefore, general principles will apply to both systems, while specific results dependent on system geometry will consider the Nanojet geometry, with comparisons drawn in cases for which the printer design has a strong impact on operation. In the same way, the experimental portion of this work will employ a silver nanoparticle ink due to its practical relevance, but the basic physical principles and models can be applied to diverse inks, including particle-free formulations. (b) An image of a Nanojet printer is displayed. (c) Simulated droplet size distributions by number and mass for xylene and water, illustrating polydispersity. Aerosol droplet generation Commercially available AJP systems employ an ultra-sonic bath for atomization of the ink. High frequency (MHz) ultrasound sets up a capillary wave on the ink surface, leading droplets to break off with a fairly well defined size distribution. The ink viscosity and amount

chunks.text: and water, illustrating polydispersity. Aerosol droplet generation Commercially available AJP systems employ an ultra-sonic bath for atomization of the ink. High frequency (MHz) ultrasound sets up a capillary wave on the ink surface, leading droplets to break off with a fairly well defined size distribution. The ink viscosity and amount determine the critical power required for atomization, as the ultrasonic wave must propagate through the liquid to the surface with limited viscous damping. The droplet size generated is related to the capillary wavelength, determined by the ultra-sound frequency, the ink density, and the ink surface tension. Based on the expected median number diameter for droplets and a log-normal distribution to model polydispersity, figure 1(c) shows idealized diameter distributions (weighted by droplet number and mass) for xylene and water, representing two inks with widely varying surface tension. Due to their micron-scale sizes, aerosol gas droplets quickly lose solvent upon contact with a dry gas stream. The resulting reduction in drop size facilitates uptake in the aerosol carrier gas stream, which is expected to become saturated with solvent vapor on a timescale of seconds under typical operating condi-tions. As a result, the droplet size is largely stable dur-ing transport from the cartridge to the deposition head, until coming into contact with the sheath gas. To prevent complete drying of aerosol droplets, it is com-mon practice to design inks with ~10% of a low-vola-tility cosolvent. This helps maintain generality of results here, droplet size will be explicitly controlled as a vari-able, and in most cases considered as a distribution. Processes that vary considerably with droplet size, then, will be strongly coupled with the ink formulation. Moreover, droplet size polydispersity will be exacerbated by dry-ing effects. Because the droplet size distribution is an important parameter for the various physical pro-cesses downstream, more detailed, process-specific modeling of aerosol evaporation will be addressed in guide ink design in future work. A more qualitative discussion is included here to preserve generality of the results while still considering the important effects coupling the droplet size with physical processes and experimental outputs.
