Aerosol transport Following atomization, the aerosol gas carries ink droplets through the mist tube to the deposition head. During this process, which can take on the order of 10s under typical operating conditions, droplets colliding with the walls are lost. Material impinging on the walls is not printed, leading to changes in the deposition rate. Moreover, as this material builds up over time, it can lead to process drift, contaminate or even clog the deposition head, and overall limit the printing lifetime. Two physical mechanisms are con-sidered here for transport losses: gravitational settling and diffusion. Broadly speaking, large droplets are more susceptible to gravitational settling, while small droplets exhibit increased diffusion, defining a win-dow of droplet sizes useful for processing. In addition to droplet size, the gas flow rate and geometry of the mist tube are key parameters. Gravitational settling is treated based on the work of Thomas. The survival probability, or fraction of droplets remaining suspended, is a function of the geometry, droplet size, and flow rate, as described by equation (1). Figure 2(a) shows the survival probability as a function of droplet size for various flow rates, based on an approximate geometry for the Nanojet system. This effect functions as a soft, low-pass filter on droplet size, and can be controlled during operation by selection of the flow rate. Intuitively, larger droplets require a high flow rate to be carried through the mist tube without settling, and even at high flow rates an appreciable fraction of aerosol droplets are lost. In practice, the survival probability can be integrated over a distribution of droplet sizes to account for polydispersity. While gravitational settling filters out large dro-plets, small droplets are more susceptible to diffusion. Here the diffusion loss of droplets is considered by assuming that droplets within a diffusion length of the tube edge impinge on the

While gravitational settling filters out large dro-plets, small droplets are more susceptible to diffusion. Here the diffusion loss of droplets is considered by assuming that droplets within a diffusion length of the tube edge impinge on the tube sidewalls and are lost. The results based on this simple model are shown in figure 2(b), indicating a decrease in transport efficiency only for very small droplets. As with gravitational settling, the system geometry is important here, with a longer mist tube leading to increased diffusion loss of droplets. Transport losses due to gravitational settling and diffusion create a processing window of suitable drop sizes, which depends on the flow rate and system geo-metry. A higher flow rate and shorter mist tube length leads to a broader window, allowing a wider range of droplet sizes through to the substrate. In effect, a longer mist tube necessitates a higher flow rate to achieve comparable transport losses, as is the case for a standard Optomec system. Many differences in printing char-acteristics between the Optomec and Nanojet systems likely stem from transport effects in coupling instru-ment design and the droplet size distribution. While transport losses are generally considered undesirable, because they can limit process throughput and print-ing lifetime, with careful system design this filtering effect could be used to better control the size distribu-tion of droplets for printing. In practice, the transport efficiency is a key factor in the deposition rate. In broad terms, the deposition rate can be related to the product of the aerosol density entering the mist tube, the aerosol flow rate, and the transport efficiency. This allows a comparison of the model with experimental results. If a nearly constant aerosol density is assumed, then nonlinearity in the deposition rate with varying aerosol flow rate can be attributed to transport loss. This is particularly impor-tant at low aerosol flow rates, for which increased gravitational settling imposes a tighter filter on the droplet size. In general, gravitational settling will dom-inate transport effects for the typical range of droplet size relevant to AJP, with larger droplets more sensitive to these effects. Higher atomizer power has been observed to produce a population of larger droplets, and inks with insufficient volatility will retain a larger droplet size, with reduced uptake into the mist tube and increased settling. Aerosol beam collimation On entering the deposition head, the aerosol gas laden with ink droplets is surrounded by a sheath gas flow. This collimates the beam, and prevents accumulation of ink on the walls of the deposition nozzle. The sheath gas is an important means for focusing the aerosol beam to achieve high precision patterning. In addition to collimating the aerosol beam by volume displace-ment, the sheath gas flow accelerates the aerosol beam through the deposition nozzle. The baseline focusing of the aerosol beam is considered here as a simple, non-mixing volume displacement (figure 3(a)). Con-sidering the parabolic velocity profile for fully devel-oped laminar pipe flow, the expected collimation can be calculated from the ratio of sheath and aerosol flow rates, or focusing ratio, as shown in equation (2). This provides a baseline estimate for the resolution, shown in figure 3(a). Notably, this is independent

This provides a baseline estimate for the resolution, shown in figure 3(a). Notably, this is independent of drop size, and therefore generalizes to different inks. In some regimes of printing, this simple estimate is surprisingly accurate, as shown in figures 3(b), (c). In particular, this is most accurate for printing with a 'wet' ink containing a high proportion of low-volatility cosol-vent. A drier ink can lead to better or worse resolution than estimated from this simple model, suggesting that this does not provide a complete description, and high flow rates lead to a consistent deviation from this behavior. As detailed next, in these printing regimes impaction effects, undeveloped flow, sheath gas-induced drying, and possible aerodynamic focusing in the deposition nozzle can account for the deviation in resolution. Aerodynamic focusing Aerodynamic lensing offers an opportunity to colli-mate the aerosol beam beyond the volume displace-ment focusing effect of the sheath gas. As the aerosol beam travels through the narrow, converging nozzle, the inertia of droplets can cause them to deviate from the gas flow streamlines. In a well-constructed aerodynamic lens, droplets can be shifted towards the flow centerline. This effect is sensitive to the droplet size and the geometry of the lens, and is widely exploited in aerosol mass spectrometry and other analytical techniques. It is common to describe effects of inertial forces using the dimensionless Stokes number, shown in equation (3). For a conventional thin-plate orifice, optimal focusing occurs for a Stokes number (St) near 1. Smaller droplets have less inertia, and therefore follow the flow streamlines more closely, leading to ineffective focusing. Larger droplets are more dramatically diverted from their initial flow streamlines, leading to over-focusing for Stokes number greater than ~2 in a typical geometry. For the weakly tapered deposition nozzle used in the Nanojet system, the target Stokes number is estimated to be ~4. The actual Stokes number is dependent on the nozzle diameter

The actual Stokes number is dependent on the nozzle diameter and droplet size, along with the flow rate. Figure 4(a) maps out the target droplet diameter meeting the condition St = 4 as a function of the nozzle diameter and flow rate. If this condition is met, collimation of the aerosol beam beyond that expected from sheath gas volume dis-placement alone is expected. Effective focusing is expected for a range of Stokes number around this critical value. Figure 4(b) shows a modified 'box plot' of the target droplet diameter (indicating St = 0.4, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0, and 8.0) as a function of flow rate through a standard nozzle with a 233 µm diameter. In addition, a box plot showing the expected droplet size distribu-tion (indicating 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 95th percentiles by mass) is shown at right. Effective lensing is expected when good overlap between these distribu-tions is maintained. This effect could account in part for the improved resolution experimentally observed using the 160 and 233 µm diameter deposition nozzles (figures 4(c)-(e)). For a larger deposition nozzle, the droplet Stokes number falls below the ideal range, leading to ineffective focusing and a resolution approaching that expected from volume displacement by the sheath gas alone (figure 3(b)). In pushing towards higher resolution, with smaller deposition nozzle size, smaller droplets are required to maintain resonance with the aerodynamic lens effect. Notably, this analysis uses approximate results from an idea-lized and basic nozzle geometry. Because this effect is important in achieving the best resolution, more refined, predictive numerical modeling accounting for the actual nozzle geometry is warranted. Moreover, these estimates are based on the assumption that droplets are initially located near the flow axis. Stronger geometric aberration of the lensing effect is expected for droplets located far off axis, as could result from a low sheath:aerosol flow ratio. Finally, polydispersity in the

Impaction Following ejection from the deposition nozzle, the aerosol droplets travel towards the substrate in an impinging jet. Qualitatively, small droplets, or those without enough inertia, are carried by the flow streamlines away from the axis of deposition. The smallest droplets do not impact the surface at all, as in a traditional inertial impactor, while droplets approaching a critical size will impact but with a broadened deposition pattern. Here this is treated following Flagan and Seinfeld based on cylind-rical stagnation flow. Figure 5(a) shows calculated droplet trajectories for a range of droplet sizes, with blue indicating 'populated' trajectories and red indicating 'vacant' trajectories arising from the sheath gas. The sheath gas increases the jet velocity, leading to higher droplet inertia, and pushes the aerosol droplets onto more central streamlines, where spreading is mini-mized. Small droplets exhibit a broad distribution pattern, a hallmark of AJP commonly referred to as overspray. The focusing efficiency describing broad-ening of the impaction pattern is a function of droplet size, nozzle diameter, and flow rates. This focusing efficiency is plotted against droplet size in figure 5(b) for constant flow rates (10/100 sccm aerosol/sheath gas flow) and several different nozzle diameters. Each curve asymptotes at the cutoff for impaction, and droplets approaching this cutoff yield a more diffuse impaction pattern. A sharper cutoff at lower diameter is calculated for the smaller diameter nozzles, due to increased flow velocity and inertia of the droplets. A distribution of droplet sizes is considered in figure 5(c), which shows the calculated line profile for different median droplet diameters. This further shows the effect of droplet size, and results in a line profile characteristic of AJP with a dense core region surrounded by diffuse overspray. The flow rate, and flow rate ratio, is also an important factor in determin-ing the final deposition profile, as the sheath gas affects both the initial beam collimation and the velocity (figure 5(d)). The flow rate, and flow rate ratio, is also an important factor in determin-ing the final deposition profile, as the sheath gas affects both the initial beam collimation and the velocity (figure 5(d)). Broadening of the impaction pattern is expected to be most severe for large diameter nozzles, low total flow rate, and low sheath:aerosol flow rate ratio. This effect is exaggerated when a drier ink is used, as small droplets are more prone impaction effects. When impaction is taken into account, the agreement between expected and experimental resolu-tion at low flow rates is considerably improved (figure 5(e)). Line broadening due to impaction effects can explain the commonly observed AJP line profile, with small droplets leading to overspray around a central, thick line. Because this effect depends strongly on the droplet size, this drives ink design. As mentioned pre-viously, a general rule of thumb is to add ~10% of a cosolvent with low-volatility to increase the droplet size, making impingement on the surface possible and reducing the overspray. As with transport losses and aerodynamic focusing, impaction depends critically on the droplet size, motivating further work to engi-neer a more refined droplet size distribution. In addi-tion to explaining features of line resolution and thickness profile, the impinging jet model has implica-tions for the deposition rate. Under certain printing conditions near the impaction cutoff, the deposition rate falls off at low sheath flow rates due to droplets not impacting the surface. Importantly, impaction effects are pri-marily dependent on the droplet Stokes number, and the target Stokes number for aerodynamic focusing is well above that for efficient impaction. Thus, if the process is engineered for aerodynamic focusing, impaction effects do not need to be considered inde-pendently. However, polydispersity in the aerosol dro-plet size distribution, especially considering the dynamic and spatially varying drying effects of the sheath gas, presents a challenge for limiting overspray effects due to impaction. Nonidealities While the mechanisms discussed thus far are relevant for proper AJP, several sources of nonideality are briefly mentioned here. First, rapid deposition of a wet ink leads to excessive fluidity on the substrate, which can lead to increased line spreading or fluid instabil-ities. In practice, this can be mitigated by increasing the printing speed and reducing the deposition rate. Deposition of a moderately dry ink can lead to an enhanced resolution, as the sheath gas dries droplets around the periphery of the aerosol stream. Once substantially dried, these droplets can fall below the critical Stokes number for impaction. Due to the micron-scale nature of the droplets, under common operating conditions in a wide-bore geometry the increase in vapor concentra-tion due to evaporation can largely offset the loss due to diffusion, leading to a sharp drying front moving radially inward. While leading to an enhanced realized resolution, this effect results in inefficient ink utilization and the generation of dry airborne particles, a concern for large-scale manufacturing and an important environ-mental safety

While leading to an enhanced realized resolution, this effect results in inefficient ink utilization and the generation of dry airborne particles, a concern for large-scale manufacturing and an important environ-mental safety and health consideration. Because this effect coincides with optimal resolution, users are prone to deliberately operate in this phase space without understanding the risks, with more material becoming airborne than is deposited on the substrate in some cases. Dry printing is also expected to influence the final morphology, in that a wet film is expected to flow to fill voids and porosity, while deposition of dry or nearly dry particles could lead to a more granular structure for certain materials. The nonideality for printing a dry ink can be addressed through ink design, commonly by employing a higher proportion of a low-volatility cosolvent. Another source of nonideality is present at high flow rates (figures 3(b), 5(e)), and could be attributed to incom-plete flow development in the deposition nozzle. This effect is observed at a similar onset flow rate for different nozzle diameters, but varies with the deposition nozzle length, supporting this conclusion. This is dependent on the geometry of the deposition nozzle, and thus the data here for a Nanojet nozzle do not translate directly to the Optomec system, while the basic mechanism would still be expected. These nonidealities or devia-tions from expected behavior are summarized in table 1, along with the primary variables affecting the key experimental outputs of deposition rate and resolution. Process limitations and optimization on printing lifetime, stable deposition is possible over extended printing runs, with line arrays printed over 3 h showing good consistency, sharp line edges, and high resolution. More generally, drift in the ink composition over time can have compounding downstream effects, coupling with transport, sheath gas-induced drying, and impaction. While several strategies have been presented for online process monitoring and control, they rely on a single experimental output and empirical correlations for feedback control. Without understanding the underlying physics leading to drift in a given output, these strategies are ill equipped to accommodate the complexity of the process. This description of AJP based on basic principles of aerosol physics and fluid mechanics provides a use-ful framework for analyzing process limitations more generally. A key benefit of AJP, and a key metric for print quality, is the line resolution. As discussed above, a baseline resolution estimate depends on the deposi-tion nozzle diameter and the focusing ratio, or sheath: aerosol flow ratio. For enhanced resolution, effective aerodynamic focusing is desired, which depends on the nozzle diameter, total flow rate, and droplet diameter. Figures 6(a) and (b) reproduce calculations for the baseline resolution and target droplet diameter for focusing, with several superimposed lines desig-nating a practical process window. Smaller nozzle dia-meter and higher sheath:aerosol flow ratio allows for a better baseline resolution. A high sheath:aerosol flow ratio is also important for aerodynamic focusing, as droplets originating far from the flow axis result in greater aberration. Practically, the sheath:aerosol flow ratio also serves to prevent droplet impingement inside the deposition nozzle. In practice, maintaining a focusing ratio of 2 or higher offers a good rule of thumb, providing a lower limit to flow on the process maps shown in figures 6(a), (b). A minimum aerosol flow rate (set by transport losses and throughput con-siderations; 6 sccm is considered here) coupled with high sheath:aerosol flow ratio and a small diameter nozzle leads to a high operating pressure, establishing another important limitation of the process. Importantly, the pressure in the deposition head scales with the flow rate (Q) and nozzle diameter (D) as Q²/D². In figures 6(a), (b), a lower limit to the nozzle diameter is established by a pressure limit of 0.2 bar. While this does not represent an absolute pressure limit, it illus-trates the scaling behavior. Notably, resolution con-tours approximately track lines of constant pressure across different nozzle diameters, indicating that, for a given limiting pressure, the optimal resolution is rela-tively invariant with the nozzle size. This is consistent with the experimental observations of Mahajan et al. It is evident that operation at low aerosol flow rates is beneficial, but this is limited in practice by the transport efficiency, a function of the printer design, and will also result in decreased throughput. In addi-tion, operation at high pressures has a feedback effect in suppressing the real aerosol flow rate, and so can increase process sensitivity before the pressure limit is reached. Another limitation for high quality AJP comes from the impaction process, in which droplets approaching the critical size are defocused. This is determined by the Stokes number, which scales as Q/D³. Notably, for smaller droplets (diameter dp), the critical nozzle dia-meter scales approximately with dp²/³Q¹/³, and thus smaller droplets require a higher flow rate and/or nar-rower nozzle to maintain a sufficiently high Stokes number. The upper limit to nozzle diameter is plotted in figures 6(a), (b), considering a 1.0 µm minimum droplet size. It is also possible to consider an upper limit to the Stokes number (lower limit to nozzle dia-meter) based on over-focusing. This would also scale with Q/D³, and largely falls below the limiting pres-sure for the case considered here. Because of this, and because this is dependent on the nozzle geometry, it is omitted from figures 6(a), (b). Finally, using the standard deposition nozzles for the Nanojet printer, an upper limit to the total flow rate is observed. This has been observed in previous studies at high flow rates, and may be due to incomplete flow development in the deposition nozzle. For the purposes here, an upper limit to the flow rate of 160 sccm is shown in figure 6(b), defining a process window for suitable AJP. This indicates a relaxed condition, as shorter deposition nozzles for the Nanojet printer often exhibit nonidealities above 80 sccm, resulting in a more constrained process window. Importantly, this effect is dependent on the nozzle geometry, and could likely be modified with minimal secondary effects. To push the concept of aero-dynamic focusing further, careful ink engineering could yield a refined droplet size distribution tuned to resonance with the nozzle. Importantly, the target Stokes number for aerodynamic focusing is dependent on the flow geometry. Thin-plate orifices, for example, have a target Stokes number of ~1, while tapered conical nozzles with a higher angle than that used here have intermediate values. In advancing the AJP technique, the possibility of incorporating multiple aerodynamic lenses upstream to sequentially focus droplets of different sizes could provide aerosol beam collimation tolerant to polydispersity in the initial droplet size distribution. This method, already used in aerosol mass spectrometry, could offer utility for high precision AJP. The basic models described here, with particular emphasis on their interrelationships, provide a strong foundation for understanding experimental outputs of AJP. Two primary measurables are deposition rate and resolution. The deposition rate is related to print-ing parameters through several mechanisms. First, the transport efficiency directly impacts the deposition rate, leading to a nonlinear increase in deposition rate with aerosol flow, and this effect is coupled with the droplet size distribution and the printer design. In addition, the sheath flow can have secondary effects on the deposition rate. At low sheath flow (and large noz-zle diameter), impaction loss leads to a decreased deposition rate. At high sheath flow (and small nozzle diameter), pressure in the deposition head suppresses the aerosol flow, with a compound effect due to transport losses. Moreover, drying of the aerosol stream on contact with the sheath gas can substantially reduce the impaction efficiency. These qualitative descriptions match well with experimental results. The resolu-tion is principally determined by the nozzle diameter and flow ratio, which provide a simple baseline esti-mate independent of the ink. Deviations from this can occur due to impaction spreading at low St, aero-dynamic focusing at moderate St, drying due to the sheath gas, and incomplete flow development in the nozzle at high flow. These effects are coupled with the droplet size, which is itself related to ink formula-tion, printer design, and process parameters (i.e., fil-tering effect of transport losses, drying due to sheath gas). Despite the complexity of the technology, it can be effectively broken down into component physical processes to establish a more comprehensive conceptual understanding. This simple framework provides a strong foundation onto which more sophis-ticated process-specific models can be built, and a valuable tool for addressing more nuanced inter-relationships affecting the AJP process. Conclusion The analysis of AJP undertaken here offers a general and accessible framework for understanding and improving the technology. By exploring several key physical processes involved in printing, complex interactions between printer design, ink formulation, and print parameter selection are revealed. Aerosol losses during transport from the cartridge to the deposition head can be considered, with effects on the deposition rate and, in some cases, the consistency over an extended print. The focusing effect of the sheath gas is described analytically based on simple volume displacement, leading to a simple relation describing a baseline resolution estimate as a function of the nozzle diameter and focusing ratio. In addition, cases for which additional aerodynamic focusing effects are expected are considered. Impaction effects can also be understood from basic models, resulting in a more refined window of process parameters for efficient printing. Moreover, with this general frame-work in place, nonidealities and deviations related to flow, pressure, and ink design can be identified and understood. Although this approach employs simple models, key experiments validate its physical rele-vance, and the relative simplicity allows relationships to be understood on an intuitive, conceptual level. Moreover, this approach identifies physical processes that are particularly important and complex, thus meriting more sophisticated modeling. For example, the droplet size distribution is important for transport, focusing, and impaction, and is a dynamic variable dependent on the ink formulation and process parameters. Furthermore, effective aerodynamic len-sing is likely to be important for pushing the limits of resolution, and numerical modeling of the specific deposition nozzle geometry would be valuable in this regard. While it is grounded in basic, analytical descriptions of key physical processes, this approach offers a strong foundation for better understanding the interrelationships between parameters and pro-cesses. Moreover, the mathematical framework pro-vides an opportunity for issues of process sensitivity and reliability to be explored. Overall, this adds a valuable component to the AJP toolbox, and marks a step towards a greater fundamental understanding characteristic of more mature printing methods.

chunks.text: The Optomec Aerosol Jet HD2 Motion and Vision Manual with KEWB provides detailed information about the system's operation, maintenance, and safety procedures, with a focus on its motion and vision capabilities. **Chapter 1: AJ System Description** **1.1 Safety Precautions** To prevent personal injury, improper operation, or system failure, it is crucial to observe safety precautions. Safety stickers are placed on the system, as detailed in document 9001016 AJ 5X, FLEX, 200, and HD2 Safety Sticker Placement. * **All systems - Deposition material:** Consult appropriate safety data sheets (SDS) for proper handling of all inks, pastes, and other materials used in the AJ system. * **Inhalation danger:** The AJ system can produce atomized particles of material that are easily inhaled. Use proper protection and ventilation when using the system. * **Gas pressure:** Adhere to the pressure ratings specified for gases introduced into the AJ system. Over-pressurizing the system can result in improper operation, system failure, or personal injury. * **Electrical shock:** The AJ HD2 system has a power distribution panel. Danger! Do not open this panel without first terminating the source power. Failure to comply with this warning may result in serious personal injury. * **Motion stages:** The high-speed movements of the AJ HD2 motion stages can cause injury. Keep arms and fingers away from the system during the deposition process. * **Optional heaters - Burn danger:** If the AJ system has a heated platen, use caution. The heated platen can reach temperatures of 120°C (248°F), causing severe burns. * **Optional UV cure module - High intensity ultraviolet light hazard:** If your system includes the UV cure module, review safety precautions and operating instructions in the user manual. Safety precautions include mandatory use of ultraviolet-blocking protective goggles or a face shield, and recommended use of long-sleeved shirts or lab coats, and ultraviolet-opaque gloves to protect hands. * **Optional laser modules - Invisible laser radiation (laser sintering tool):** Danger: Laser radiation when open and interlock defeated. Avoid eye or skin exposure to direct or scattered radiation. * **Invisible laser radiation – laser distance sensor:** Caution: Laser radiation when open and interlock defeated.

Any variable expression can be monitored against custom values or ranges. A background poller continuously checks and reports alarms. When triggered, an alarm can display a message, pause/abort motion, or run embedded commands. The poller and enabled alarms from the last exit start automatically on program startup. Note: The poller status "Last Update" time continuously updates when the poller is active. The alarm configuration interface uses a spreadsheet-like format. Each row (1) represents an alarm, with cells containing user-defined properties. Menus (2) offer options to add new alarms, restart an inactive poller, and define system variable options. The bottom (3) shows the poller's current status, including the last update time. Some alarms are read-only (XML editable) and have a red background. When an alarm's conditions are met, it triggers and appears on the Alarms Screen, requiring acknowledgment. Additional actions may occur. While triggered, the poller does not evaluate it. After acknowledgment, it re-enables, and polling resumes. **3.4.1 Alarm Properties and Components** Each alarm has properties and components; invalid fields show a red exclamation point. * **Enabled:** Check to activate the alarm, continuously monitoring trigger conditions. The KEWB Maintenance > Engineer > Lighting tab has ON/OFF and intensity controls for visible light LEDs. The master power button controls all LEDs, and a scale below it controls their intensity. These can also be controlled via the KEWB sequencer. Each LED (left and right) can be individually controlled by its light icon (ON/OFF) and scale (intensity). LED intensity saves upon closing if ON; otherwise, it defaults to 0. **3.7 Adjust the Z Height and Focus the Cameras** The HD2™ deposition head and camera on the AJ HD2 system are statically mounted to the Z payload. Adjust the payload height relative to the substrate. **3.7.1 Adjust the HD2™ Deposition Head Nozzle Height** Adjust the deposition head height so the nozzle is 2 to 5 mm above the substrate. If using a wide nozzle: 1. Ensure the deposition head's vertical position clears the platen and workpiece. 2. Navigate to KEWB Maintenance > Engineer > X and Y jog buttons to move the platen under the nozzle. 3. Turn the key-switch to Bypass mode. 4. Press the blue Reset button on the operator panel. 5. Open the enclosure door. 6. Arrange three microscope slides on the workpiece, offsetting the top slide to tilt away if touched by the nozzle. 7. Adjust the deposition head assembly so the nozzle is at the appropriate height: i. Turn the key-switch back to Bypass Off. ii. Use the KEWB Z Movement Tools to adjust nozzle height. iii. When the nozzle is within 1 mm of the slides, select Jog speed > Slow. iv. Slowly adjust the nozzle to the appropriate height. **3.7.2 Focus the Process Camera** Once the deposition head is at the correct height, focus the process camera: 1. In the vision window, press the Live Process Feed button. 2. Use the process camera’s focus knob to slowly adjust until the clearest image is visible in the KEWB vision window. Note: Because the process camera is angled, only part of the image will be in focus. **3.7.3 Focus the Alignment Camera** The alignment camera is the reference for other tools. 1. In Vision, under the Lighting tab, turn ON the alignment camera ring light. 2. Navigate to KEWB Maintenance > Engineer > X and Y movement tools to move the platen until the alignment camera is above your workpiece. 3. In the vision window, press Vertical Live Feed. 4. Navigate to KEWB Maintenance > Engineer > Z movement tools to slowly adjust the focus until the clearest image is seen in the Vision Manager. **3.7.4 Camera Mounting Tool** A 0.035” Allen wrench is required to mount and unmount the alignment and process cameras.

Navigate to KEWB Maintenance > Engineer > Z movement tools to slowly adjust the focus until the clearest image is seen in the Vision Manager. **3.7.4 Camera Mounting Tool** A 0.035” Allen wrench is required to mount and unmount the alignment and process cameras. **3.8 Vision Inspections** Vision inspections are used in the software to locate products and align printing. An inspection involves a Cognex VisionPro® QuickBuild® file with a single QuickBuild® job that captures and processes images to report results, usually coordinates for fixturing toolpaths. Inspections can also measure part features like printed line widths. Positions, when calibrated, are relative to the camera's location. All camera image processing uses Cognex VisionPro® QuickBuild® software with an OakRiver Technology driver package. VisionPro® handles communication, image capture, and processing. Inspections are edited directly in QuickBuild® (accessed from Vision tab in Maintenance menu). Refer to Cognex VisionPro® documentation for detailed information. **3.8.1 Creating a new inspection** Inspections are typically created by saving and modifying existing ones or by opening VisionPro® QuickBuild® directly from the Windows® start menu. Most inspections require two layered calibrations for real-world coordinates instead of pixels: 1. **CogCalibCheckerboardTool1:** A checkerboard calibration providing lens corrections and scaling, based on a NIST traceable checkerboard slide. 2. **CogCalibNPointToNPointTool2:** An n-point calibration rotating the coordinate system to match real-world stage coordinates. Part locating tools (e.g., CogPMAlignTool for feature location/rotation via pattern matching) are placed after calibrations. A CogResultsAnalysisTool, named "Results," is added at the end to pass results to the sequencer. Inspections can be tested directly from the QuickBuild® editor. The new inspection must be added to `VisionProInspections.xml` in `C:\AerosolJetPrinter\Config` using a new `<Inspection>` XML tag with a unique index. The user interface must be restarted for the added inspection to appear. **3.8.2 Editing Inspections** Inspections are edited by clicking the "Edit" button on the Vision tab in the Maintenance screen. **3.8.3 Removing Inspections** Inspections are removed by deleting them from the `VisionProInspections.xml` file in `C:\AerosolJetPrinter\Config`. They will no longer appear in the user interface after a restart. **3.8.4 VisionProInspections.xml Schema Information** Inspections are loaded from `VisionProInspections.xml`. *

They will no longer appear in the user interface after a restart. **3.8.4 VisionProInspections.xml Schema Information** Inspections are loaded from `VisionProInspections.xml`. * **Global settings within `<Global>` XML tag:** * **`<CalTool>`:** Defines default calibration tool type for all inspections. Values can be "NPoint," "Checkerboard," or "Fixture" (Advanced). Default is "Checkerboard." Only applies to inspections that are the source of a `<CalData>`. * **`<MinDriveSpaceFree>`:** Minimum free drive space in megabytes to save an image. Default is 500. * **`<SaveWithToolsImageFormat>`:** Default image format to use when saving with tools. Default is "PNG." * **Inspection settings within an `<Inspection>` XML tag:** * **`<VisionFile>`:** The inspection file to load (*.vpp). **Required.** * **`<CalTool>`:** Defines calibration tool type for this inspection. Default is "Value from <Global> Section." * **`<VProSaveImage>`:** Image from VisionPro inspection to use when saving. Default is "ImageSource.OutputImage." * **`<VProDisplayImage>`:** Image from VisionPro inspection to use for displaying. Default is "ImageSource.OutputImage." * **`<CalData>`:** Inspection number containing calibration data. This inspection's calibration data will be replaced by the provided number. Default is "None." * **`<CalDataSource>`:** When updating calibration, this inspection number identifies the source to copy and reload. Default is "None." * **`<CalData>` (with Number attribute, e.g., `<CalData Number="2">`):** Inspection number of the Nth CalDataAndVerification inspection where calibrations are stored, used only for inspections requiring multiple calibrations. Default is "None." * **`<SaveWithToolsImageFormat>`:** Image format for saving with tools. Default is "Value from <Global> Section." **3.8.5 Calibrations** Cameras are automatically calibrated by running the calibration sequence. Each camera used for measurement has two calibration sets: 1. **Pixel space to real-world dimensions:** Computed against a checkerboard pattern. 2. **Motion to camera:** Corrects for checkerboard rotation in its mounting block. Motion-to-camera calibration is stacked on checkerboard calibration for maximum accuracy. These calibrations are in multiple vision files: * **Calibration compute inspection:** Calculates image transforms for calibration. For checkerboard, it finds all corners. For n-point, it maps 13 stage positions to camera locations and computes a transform. * **Calibration measure inspection:**

These calibrations are in multiple vision files: * **Calibration compute inspection:** Calculates image transforms for calibration. For checkerboard, it finds all corners. For n-point, it maps 13 stage positions to camera locations and computes a transform. * **Calibration measure inspection:** Measures checkerboard slide features and compares them to NIST traceable measurements, ensuring successful calibration. Transforms are linked to those of the compute inspection. * **Calibration data and verification inspection:** Stores calibration results for normal operation and allows checking if the camera setup has changed, invalidating the calibration. **3.8.6 Inspection Inputs and Outputs** Inspections can take inputs and return measurements. * **Inputs:** A CogToolGroup named "Inputs" must be created, containing script terminal outputs (e.g., Input_1, Input_2) with "Double" data type. The software passes as many inputs as exist. * **Outputs:** Results are returned via a CogResultsAnalysisTool named "Results," created at the end of the job. Add desired results as inputs to this tool. They are passed back to the software in the order listed. Arrays are supported for inputs and will fill slots sequentially. **Chapter 4: Sequencer** The machine sequencer provides a graphical programming interface for engineers to develop sequences that define machine operations. Capabilities include: * Operator prompting, decisions, and inputs. * Program looping and logical sequence control. * Coordinated motion control. * Digital and analog input/output control. * Print head control, ink recipe control, configurable alarm control, mass flow controller control, heater control, syringe pump control. * Vision: calibrations, product detection/location, real-time images, and live feed display. Users can create unlimited sequences, stored in XML files in the configuration folder. **4.1 Running Sequences** An operator runs one sequence at a time by pressing the "Start" button on the Main Screen. The selection prompt shows sequences whose "Start Conditions" are met. The sequence selection prompt lists all runnable sequences, with descriptions and optional images for quick identification. To start, select from the list and press "Proceed." When the software starts, it runs the "Reset" sequence (defined on the Sequences Screen with the name "Reset"). This sequence should move the machine

This sequence should move the machine from any unknown setup to a known safe state for running other sequences. **4.2 Overview** A sequence is a list of steps the machine runs sequentially. Steps are defined by selecting an available step type and assigning parameters, covering motion, print head control, operator interactions, and vision. Step types also enable jumping, looping, and conditional structures based on device states or variables. **4.2.1 Variables and Expressions** Most numeric parameters in the sequencer can be set to a variable's value or an expression of numeric variables from the Variables Screen. Entry boxes auto-suggest available variables and allow arbitrary expressions and constants. Equations are parsed by mXparser, supporting common math functions (sin, cos, etc.). **4.2.2 String Formatting** Most operator prompts and text messages can embed variable values using Interpolated Strings and the data type's .NET format string. Example: `Error 1: {User_Error1:0.000} mm` will replace `User_Error1` with its value, formatted to 3 decimal places (e.g., `Error 1: 0.025 mm`). **4.2.3 Labels** Labels are special sequence steps that define jump points, enabling loops and branches by skipping normal sequential execution. They are created with the "Sequencing – Label" step type and named. Many sequence steps use label names for conditional jumps. If a label parameter is "N/A," the next step executes. A special "End of Sequence" label always exists to complete execution. **4.3 User Interface** Sequences are developed graphically on the HMI Sequences Screen. **4.3.1 Sequence List** The starting point for editing sequences, listing all existing sequences and allowing editing, duplicating, or creating new ones. chunks.text: Types:** * **Alarm Control:** Start/stop monitoring Configurable Alarms. * **Flow Control:** Changes setpoints on mass flow controllers. * **Temperature Control:** Sets heater target temperatures. * **Home Syringe Pump:** Homes the syringe pump. * **Recipe Control:** Start/stop an ink recipe. * **Syringe Pump Control:** Changes dispense mode and/or dispense rate of a syringe pump. * **Sequencing Step Types:** * **Alarm:** Triggers an alarm, putting machine into faulted (paused) state, message on alarms screen. * **Check Variables:** Compares variable(s) to limits and jumps to pass/fail labels. * **Delay:** Waits for a pre-defined duration. * **Jump to Label:** Jumps to the specified Sequencing – Label step. * **Label:** Label definition to change sequence execution order. * **Run Other Sequence:** Runs another sequence and waits for completion. * **Set Variables:** Writes a value to variable(s) (constant, other variable, or expression). * **Wait for Variables:** Waits until variable(s) are within limits or timeout is reached. * **Part Data Step Types:** * **Data Log Control:** Controls CSV data logger (start/stop and variable specification). * **Log Part Data:** Logs specified variables to a CSV file. **4.5.1 Motion – Actuator Control** Extends or retracts the selected actuator and waits for completion. * **Actuator:** Selects actuator to control. * **Action:** "Extend" moves to extended position, "Retract" moves to retracted position. **4.5.2 Motion – Analog Output Control** Sets specified analog outputs to new output levels. * **Analog output to control:** Selects analog output. * **New value:** Defines new output level in analog output units. **4.5.3 Motion – Crash Zone Control** Enables or disables crash zone monitoring. Used when components are added/removed to match crash zones to installed components. Crash zones are set via `CrashZones.xml`. * **Crash zone to control:** Name of crash zone to enable/disable. * **Enabled?:** Whether crash zone is enabled/disabled. **4.5.4 Motion – Define Fixture** Redefines the active coordinate system for motion and toolpaths. New coordinate offsets are in local coordinates with unity parameters, not stacked. Rotations are centered about the new fixture center (X, Y, Z offsets). chunks.text: coordinate system for motion and toolpaths. New coordinate offsets are in local coordinates with unity parameters, not stacked. Rotations are centered about the new fixture center (X, Y, Z offsets). Transformations combine in this order: XY Stage Squareness, Z Stage Squareness (XZ and YZ squareness), Stage Scaling, XYZ Offsets, XYZ Scaling, rotation about Y, then Z axis. Rotation about X is applied to the A axis. Z-axis rotation is about the new Z' axis after Y rotation. * **X offset:** Translation of new coordinate system in X-axis. * **Y offset:** Translation of new coordinate system in Y-axis. * **Z offset:** Translation of new coordinate system in Z-axis. * **Rotation about X:** Rotation of new coordinate system about X-axis. * **Rotation about Y:** Rotation of new coordinate system about Y-axis. * **Rotation about Z:** Rotation of new coordinate system about Z-axis. * **X scaling:** Scaling of new coordinate system in X-axis. * **Y scaling:** Scaling of new coordinate system in Y-axis. * **Z scaling:** Scaling of new coordinate system in Z-axis. Additionally, `Motion_StageScalingX`, `Motion_StageScalingY`, `Motion_StageScalingZ`, `Motion_StageSquarenessXY`, `Motion_StageSquarenessXZ`, and `Motion_StageSquarenessYZ` machine variables are applied to the fixture on every call. These persistent variables correct for stage manufacturing and mounting errors. When using MasterCAM® toolpaths, X, Y, Z offsets should ensure the print nozzle prints at the toolpath origin. This is usually not the start of the first trace. * **Example: Start a toolpath from current location with no additional scaling or rotations.** * X offset: `Motion_X_ActualPosition` * Y offset: `Motion_Y_ActualPosition` * Z offset: `Motion_Z_ActualPosition` * Rotation about X, Y, Z: 0 * X, Y, Z scaling: 1 * **Example: Start a toolpath from a vision location determined from two measured points.** * `User_PartX1`, `User_PartY1`, `User_PartZ1`: vision measurements of X, Y, Z coordinates of one part location, converted to stage coordinates. * `User_PartX2`, `User_PartY2`, `User_PartZ2`: vision measurements of X, Y, Z coordinates of a second part location, converted to stage coordinates. * `User_PartA`: Directly measured angle of product by horizontal camera. * `User_OffsetX`, `User_OffsetY`, `User_OffsetZ`: Offset between middle of two vision features and toolpath origin. * `User_PrintToVerticalCameraX`, `User_PrintToVerticalCameraY`, `User_PrintToVerticalCameraZ`: Offsets between ink deposition

"None" means not copied. **4.5.10 Motion – Move** Performs a coordinated linear move from the current to target location. If an approach is defined, a three-part move is performed: first, the approach axis moves past the final location; second, other axes move to their final locations; finally, the approach axis moves to its final location. This prevents crashes (e.g., nozzle hitting product). * **Coordinate system:** Selects axis group to move (automatically selected). * **Location:** Selects predefined location (Landmarks dropdown) or "Custom." Tip: Recipe control saves the directory path of selected recipe file for future use. * **Stop recipe:** * `(stop)`: Stops recipe execution. * **View recipe progress:** * **Progress bar:** Graphically displays overall recipe progress. Note: If recipe uses looping, progress bar follows the loop pattern, possibly indicating completion then restarting. **Recipe commands:** Commands are created using signal references. * **Process control electronics language:** e.g., `$SM,130,1000` translates to "Set MFC with address 130 to a value of 1000." * **Signal reference:** e.g., `Atomizer_MFC = 1000` translates to "Set Atomizer_MFC (variable defined in KPC_Preferences.xml) to a value of 1000." **Signal references:** Use simple mathematical expressions to assign values to signals, without needing native commands or exact addresses. * Value of a variable can be changed with arithmetic operators (*, /, +, -). * Standard order of operation is followed if parentheses are not used. * Exponents can be used (e.g., 5E-10 is 5*10^-10). Signals for Process controls are defined as variables in `Process_Configuration.xml` in the root `AerosolJetPrinter Config` directory. **User-defined variables:** Two types of variables are defined within a recipe: INT and REAL (both single-precision floating-point). Names must be unique and are not case-sensitive. Note: Comments start with an exclamation point and are ignored. Example: `! INT example: INT COUNT COUNT = 0` Example: `! REAL example: REAL LowPressureLimit LowPressureLimit = 0.005` Important: A user-defined variable cannot use the same name as an existing signal variable. **Display message command:** Adds a display message box to a recipe. Example: `Disp Kewa is cool` **Conditional structures:** * **IF, END:** Specifies a condition that must be met for commands between IF and END to execute. If condition is True, commands run; if False, they are ignored. Both statements required. Example: `IF Sheath_PT < 1 WAIT 1000 END` * **WHILE, END:** Specifies a condition to stop executing commands between WHILE and END. Commands run repeatedly until condition is False. Both statements

chunks.text: IF and END to execute. If condition is True, commands run; if False, they are ignored. Both statements required. Example: `IF Sheath_PT < 1 WAIT 1000 END` * **WHILE, END:** Specifies a condition to stop executing commands between WHILE and END. Commands run repeatedly until condition is False. Both statements required. Example: `REAL ROW ROW = 0 WHILE ROW < 10 ROW = ROW + 1 WAIT 1000 END` * **LOOP, END:** Repeats commands between LOOP and END for a fixed number of times or until a condition is True. Both statements required. Example 1 (fixed repetitions): `REAL ROW ROW = 0 LOOP 10 ROW = ROW + 1 WAIT 1000 END` Example 2 (repeats until condition True): `ROW = 0 LOOP ROW < 10 ROW = ROW + 1 WAIT 1000 END` Tip: Keep nesting simple; it's easy to lose track. **Closed loop control:** Recipe control (and external devices) can monitor process parameters for closed-loop control. For example, maintaining sheath pressure by dynamically adjusting sheath gas flow. This approach uses system pressure to define flow parameters, not exact values. Establish atomization/focusing starting points, then allow subtle changes. Use with caution; rapid response can cause oscillation. Example illustrates closed loop control (fictitious values): `S_MFC = 50 WAIT 10000` `! Fine tune sheath flow WHILE S_PT < .6 S_MFC = S_MFC + 5 WAIT 2000 END` `! Set a base value for Atomizer flow and wait 10 s to allow pressure to start to stabilize ATM_MFC = 200 WAIT,10000` `! Set Exhaust flow for a fixed extraction IF ATM_MFC > 30 VI_EX_MFC = ATM_MFC - 30 END` `! Fine tune Atomizer flow WHILE ATOMIZER_PT < .3 ATM_MFC = ATM_MFC + 5 VI_EX_MFC = ATM_MFC - 30 WAIT 2000 END` `! Adjust Atomization to maintain Sheath pressure but only if there is some Atomizer Flow ! If the Atomizer drops below 100 the recipe will exit the while loop and finish. WHILE ATM_MFC > 100` `! slightly lower Atomizer flow rate and exhaust IF S_PT > .7 ATM_MFC = ATM_MFC – 1 VI_EX_MFC = ATM_MFC – 30 WAIT 5000 END` `! slightly

chunks.text: ON. **Chapter 7: Conveyor (optional)** **7.1 Overview** The conveyor transports rectangular PCBs, trays, or carriers through the HD2, allowing installation on SMT production lines. It accommodates board sizes from 70-290 mm length/width and up to 25 mm height, with max weight 4 pounds. Workpieces should not have protruding components on the underside. The conveyor has a SMEMA interface for upstream/downstream communication. An upstream machine signals readiness to send a board, which the HD2 accepts when ready. The HD2 then signals readiness to send the board to the downstream machine, and sends it when accepted. **7.1.1 Gripper and XZ actuators** The gripper picks up boards and places them on the heated vacuum platen. Its fingers adjust to board width and act as guide rails. The gripper is attached to XZ actuators, allowing boards to be moved. **7.1.2 Roller sections** Two roller sections accept boards from upstream and send them downstream. A board fully inside the HD2 contacts the board end stop, squaring up with gripper rails for alignment. **7.1.3 Laser shutter doors** Shutter doors protect users from laser beams and help contain printed materials. They open/close for board passage and have spring-loaded safety mechanisms. Interlocks ensure doors are closed during normal operation; they trigger an alarm and prevent laser firing if open. **7.2 Homing** **7.2.1 Gripper and XZ actuators** XZ actuators have limit sensors for homing and preventing travel beyond allowable space. Homing is done via the "Home" button in the conveyor user interface. The "Homing Required" indicator shows if homing is needed. **7.3 Running your first board** **7.3.1 Setup** 1. Place the HD2 in-line with upstream and downstream machines. Ensure machines are leveled and conveyor sections align. The front edge of the board should align 1.8” from the front edge of the roller section. 2. Determine conveyor direction by changing the `xml key` value (`true` or `false`) in `Process_Configuration.xml` (located in `C:\AerosolJetPrinter\Config`). 3. Connect upstream and downstream machines to the back of the HD2 utility cabinet using the provided cable (PN: 8003648). **7.4 Engineer mode** **7.4.1 Jog controls** In Engineer mode, the conveyor UI allows jogging components. Set board length/width

Connect upstream and downstream machines to the back of the HD2 utility cabinet using the provided cable (PN: 8003648). **7.4 Engineer mode** **7.4.1 Jog controls** In Engineer mode, the conveyor UI allows jogging components. Set board length/width via "Settings." Select speed via "Speed" button. Shuttle gripper using "Shuttle" controls (up, down, left, right). Jog gripper fingers in/out (width specified in "Settings"). To jog rollers, select correct rollers, then jog left/right. To open/close laser shutter doors, select door, then use control button (does not jog). **Conveyor UI buttons and functions:** * **Home:** Triggers conveyor homing, moving each axis to limit position and placing conveyor in safe position. * **Load:** Places a board onto the platen from the rollers. * **Unload:** Places a board onto the platen from the rollers. * **Stop:** Stops current movement/action, indicates Error. * **Clears:** Clears error conditions. * **Length and width:** Defines board dimensions. * **Speed:** Defines speed for Jog actions (Load/Unload move at fast speed). * **Position (Left, Platen, Right):** Resets factory-defined load/unload positions. Jog to specific location, fine tune with 'slow' jogging, select position button to set. Calibrated position used for subsequent actions. **7.5 Safety** For daily operation, the operator panel key switch must be "O" - Normal. This enables laser shutter door interlock switches. If broken outside normal operation, interlocks disable motion, UV Cure LEDs, laser distance sensor, and laser sintering module. Refer to "Safety Precautions" in "AJ System Description" for more. **7.6 Conveyor turn off** To use the system without the conveyor, select the 'Safe' position to move the CCS (Conveyor Control System) to an out-of-the-way location. **7.7 Alignment** Proper conveyor functioning requires alignment. Aligned conveyor allows gripper fingers to fit in platen slots and contour rollers. **7.7.1 Conveyor alignment criteria** Conveyor is properly aligned when: 1. No gaps exist between gripper rails and 7006763 (alignment jig). Rails are parallel to each other and perpendicular to platen slots. 2. No gap between end of 7006763 and gripper rails. Fingers are parallel and centered on platen slots. 3. When positioned on

In Engineer Mode, set board width to 89 mm in conveyor UI. 2. Position gripper on platen in conveyor UI. 3. Place 7006763 onto platen, part number facing up, alignment features slotted. 4. Loosen two screws at either end of gripper connecting rails to carriages. 5. Press "gripper close" button in conveyor UI. 6. Once no gaps between jig and gripper rails, tighten four screws. 7. If both gripper rails have same-sized gap with platen top (as shown in Figure 124), skip. Set board width to 290 mm in conveyor UI. 10. Position gripper over left roller section, remove side panel. 11. Loosen screws (Figure 129) and adjust roller section until gripper rails contour rollers properly. 12. Repeat previous two steps for right roller section. **7.8 Recommended maintenance** To ensure proper functionality and longevity, perform maintenance: * **Every 3 to 6 months (standard-use):** * Wipe board-presence sensors on both roller sections. * Wipe all rollers with water and dishwashing soap. * In Engineer Mode, close laser shutter doors and check for light leaks. Doors should flush with roller section sides, blocking light from HD2's laser. * With conveyor power off or EMO pressed, turn gripper lead screws and check for binding (should spin freely). * Check conveyor alignment as per "Conveyor alignment criteria"; perform "Alignment procedure" if necessary. * **Every 1 to 3 months (severe-use):** Perform all above tasks. **7.9 Error recovery** * **Jogging into a

Press Software E-STOP/Physical E-STOP pushbutton. 2. If physical E-STOP pressed, reset it, wait 30 seconds. 3. Press "Clear Error" on Conveyor UI. 4. Press "Home" on conveyor UI. * **Collisions that physically damage the conveyor:** Contact Optomec customer support. * **Electrical faults resulting in system malfunctions:** Contact Optomec customer support. **Chapter 8: Preventative Maintenance** **8.1 Safety System** The machine has a safety system with E-stop buttons, guard door interlock, and side panel interlocks. All interlocks must be satisfied for system movement (unless Interlock Bypass key is on). Periodically open/close guard doors to confirm interlock circuit function. Check interlock mounting bolts for tightness. Check viewing windows for defects. Press E-stop button to confirm E-stop circuit function. * **Recommended frequency:** Once a month. **8.2 Electrical Surge Protection Device** The AC electrical cabinet contains an AC power surge protection device to clamp high voltage surges. If damaged by a surge, a visual fault indicator will illuminate, requiring replacement. Check regularly. * **Recommended frequency:** Once every 3 months. **8.3 Stage Guide Rails and Ballscrew** The X, Y, and Z axes stage bearings require periodic re-lubrication for optimal performance. * **Guide rails (X, Y, Z):** Lubricate every 6 months using Lamora D 68 (light mineral oil). * **Ballscrew (Z-axis):** Lubricate every 6 months using Staburags NBU 12/300 KP. * **Recommended frequency:** Once every 6 months. **8.4 Decommissioning** When decommissioning, follow all regulations, paying attention to hazardous materials in electrical components. chunks.text: Aerosol Jet™ Health and Safety Guidelines The purpose of this document is to outline health and safety guidelines for the safe handling and disposal of nanoparticles utilized or generated during the use of Aerosol Jet deposition technology. 1 Electrical Safety Do not operate the ultrasonic atomizer (or produce aerosol) without a material vial installed. Avoid contact with the water or ink spout generated by the ultrasonic atomizer. 2 Chemical Safety The ASTM Committee on Nanotechnology has defined a nanoparticle as a particle with lengths in two or three dimensions between 1 and 100 nanometers (nm). Nanoparticles can be composed of many different base materials and may be of different shapes including: nanotubes; nanowires; and crystalline structures such as fullerenes and quantum dots. Nanoparticles present a unique challenge from an occupational health perspective as there is a limited amount of toxicological data currently available for review. However, some studies have shown that existing exposure control technologies have been effective in reducing exposure to nanoparticles. As such, the accepted exposure control hierarchy was utilized in the development of this document. Types of chemicals used in the Aerosol Jet process: The types of chemicals used in the Aerosol Jet process include: Acids (cleaning), Bases (surface modification), Organic solvents, Powders and nano-materials, Organometallic precursors, Miscellaneous materials (polymers, solder pastes, flux, adhesives, etc.), and Aerosols containing the materials listed above. Risks The primary routes of exposure for nanoparticles are inhalation, dermal absorption, and ingestion. Nanoparticles or nanomaterials used in laboratory experiments will likely be in one of three forms: a powder, in suspension, or in a solid matrix. The form of the nanoparticles or nanomaterial will play a large role in the exposure potential. For example, a nanoparticle in powdered form will present a larger inhalation hazard potential than a nanoparticle in suspension. Some common tasks that present some potential for exposure include: * Working with nanoparticles in suspension without gloves; * Working with nanoparticles in suspension during pouring or mixing where agitation is involved; * Generating nanoparticles in the gas-phase; * Handling nanoparticle powders; * Maintenance on equipment used to produce nanoparticles; * Cleaning

chunks.source: AJ Health and Safety Guidelines (OEM P/N 9000876)

chunks.text: tasks that present some potential for exposure include: * Working with nanoparticles in suspension without gloves; * Working with nanoparticles in suspension during pouring or mixing where agitation is involved; * Generating nanoparticles in the gas-phase; * Handling nanoparticle powders; * Maintenance on equipment used to produce nanoparticles; * Cleaning up spills or waste material; * Cleaning dust collection systems; and * Machining, sanding, grinding, or mechanically disturbing nanomaterial which can generate an aerosol. Risk Mitigation The Aerosol Jet system comes equipped with an interlocked hood and outside ventilation ports (refer to Aerosol Jet Exhaust System slides). * The hood must be connected to a customer's external ventilation system, typically with HEPA filters used in the ventilation pathway. * Exhaust: 152 mm (6 inch) OD Tubing; 4,585 SLPM (162 SCFM) – Exhaust to HEPA Filter or House External Exhaust * The Hood Doors MUST REMAIN CLOSED during the deposition process. Any attempt to override the interlock system could cause POTENTIAL HARM to a user who may inadvertently inhale nanoparticle materials or solvent fumes. The concentration of hazardous aerosols inside the enclosure may take significant time to decay to a safe level after deposition is halted. This decay time depends on the deposition process and materials. Users should measure the exposure levels for their specific operation. Always carefully read the material MSDS information prior to loading, printing, and unloading material (ink) into the aerosol jet system. Safety Training Safety training should be considered and/or implemented in conjunction with your Aerosol Jet deposition system, focusing on employee training and proper work procedures including: * Providing known information to workers and students on the hazardous properties of the nanomaterial precursors or products; * Education of workers on the safe handling of nanomaterials; * Restricting access to areas by using signs or placards to identify areas of nanoparticle research; * Transport dry nanomaterials in closed containers; * Handle nanoparticles in suspension on disposable bench covers; * Always perform nanoparticle aerosol generating activities in a fume hood, externally ducted biological safety cabinet, or glove box; and * Clean the nanomaterial work area daily at a

chunks.text: identify areas of nanoparticle research; * Transport dry nanomaterials in closed containers; * Handle nanoparticles in suspension on disposable bench covers; * Always perform nanoparticle aerosol generating activities in a fume hood, externally ducted biological safety cabinet, or glove box; and * Clean the nanomaterial work area daily at a minimum with a HEPA-vacuum or wet wiping method. * Wear latex or nitrile gloves when handling nanoparticle powders and nanoparticles in suspension (glove changes should be performed frequently); * Wear chemical splash goggles when working with nanomaterials in suspension or dry powdered form; * Wear lab coats. Lab coats should be laundered on a periodic basis. Do not take lab coats home for laundering; * Wear commercially available arm sleeves in situations where dermal contact with nanoparticles in powder or in suspension are expected; * Wear closed-toe shoes (if necessary cover shoes with commercially available booties); * Consult with internal company policies regarding the use of respiratory protection if an inhalation exposure hazard exists. Containment (chemicals should be present only where necessary) * Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) must be worn as needed * Consult the MSDS for inks and solvents for the recommended PPE * All chemicals should be handled, stored, and disposed of properly * Food and drink are not allowed in the laboratory areas * Since the toxicology and environmental fate of nanoparticles is still largely unknown, all nanoparticle waste (solid material and liquids) should be conservatively managed as hazardous waste. This also includes any debris (i.e. PPE, plastic) that has become heavily contaminated with nanoparticles. All nanoparticle waste must be placed in an appropriate container and labeled. * All spills involving nanoparticles should be treated like a hazardous material spill and cleaned up immediately. If a spill presents an emergency situation please follow your company posted health and safety guidelines. 3 Environmental Safety Thermal * The heated substrate platen may pose a thermal safety hazard * The platen may be heated to as high as 120 °C * Take care to avoid direct contact with the heated platen during part alignment and equipment mounting Respiratory * Respiratory

chunks.text: and safety guidelines. 3 Environmental Safety Thermal * The heated substrate platen may pose a thermal safety hazard * The platen may be heated to as high as 120 °C * Take care to avoid direct contact with the heated platen during part alignment and equipment mounting Respiratory * Respiratory hazards may exist in the form of aerosolized materials and/or chemical vapors * Use an axillary exhaust system to remove aerosols when necessary * Vapors and aerosolized liquids should not be inhaled * Typically, open chemical containers should be handled under a fume hood Consult the MSDS and applicable safety recommendations for guidance E.g. OSHA Table Z-1 at: https://www.osha.gov/pls/oshaweb/owadisp.show document?p_table=standards&p_id=9992 4 Pressure Safety Under typical conditions, the Aerosol Jet apparatus operates at pressures ranging from approximately 1 to 10 psi. The gas source however may be pressurized to several thousand psi. Care should be taken to avoid over-pressurizing the system. All portable gas sources should be secured. 5 Mechanical Safety The Aerosol Jet System has both automatic and manual motion control stages that are capable of high-speed operations that can injure personnel. Keep arms and fingers away from the system during the deposition process. All motion can be stopped by depressing the emergency stop bottom on the emergency override panel. 6 Disclaimer The data contained in this Health and Safety section is believed to be true and accurate, but is offered solely for your consideration, investigation, and verification. Our systems meet U.S. OSHA safety threshold levels for an 8-hour TWA; however, there are concerns about exposure before this time period. Optomec would like to caution its customers to consult the MSDS for each material they use in either system to ensure that safety recommendations are followed. Also, follow the safety labels and warnings in the manuals and the systems themselves. Aerosol Jet Etching (AJE) – Efficiencies of laboratory-fabricated silicon solar cells (25%)1,2 significantly exceed those of typical commercial screen-printed cells (16-18%). – Need to replace photolithographic dielectric patterning processes (used by the high efficiency laboratory cells) with cheaper processes. – Photolithographic patterning of dielectric layers involves patterning of a resist layer followed by immersion etching. – When compared with immersion etching processes, AJE offers: • Fewer steps; • Uses small amounts of inexpensive chemicals and produces less hazardous F waste; and • Safer than existing immersion etching processes in that HF is only formed locally where etching is required. Process Schematic: 1. Coat with polymer layer (Polyacrylic acid, acidic, water-soluble polymer, SiO2 or SiNx, on Si substrate). 2. Deposit F- source (Aerosol containing fluoride ions acts as active etchant on the coated substrate). 3. Rinse in DI H₂O to reveal the digital etching pattern on the Si substrate. chunks.section: • What are your most common aerosol jet printing inks
chunks.text: • What are your most common aerosol jet printing inks? • Our standard conductive ink is Novacentrix Metalon JS-A426 and can be printed straight from the bottle without dilution, our standard insulating/dielectric ink is a 2:1 ratio of acetone and Norland NEA 121 which is a common, commercially available electronics adhesive • What is the viscosity range compatible with aerosol jet printing? • For ultrasonic atomization, target inks in the range of 1-10 cP (water-blood), for pneumatic atomization, aim for 1-100cp (water-oil) • What temperature is needed to cure/sinter silver ink? • You can sinter silver ink in at 100°C for 12 hours, 185° C for 4 hours, 250 deg. C for 10 minutes. Ensure that the sintering conditions will not damage the substrate or other circuit components that will exposed to the same heat, choose a lower temperature and longer time if you are unsure about the thermal limits of your system • What are some common solvents used in aerosol jet print ink formulation? • Deionized water, acetone, isopropanol (IPA), toluene, propylene glycol methyl ether acetate (PGMEA), N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), and terpineol are all common solvents used in aerosol jet printing. It is important to match the added solvent to the existing ink solvent system for compatibility. • What is the ideal standoff distance for an aerosol jet printing nozzle? • The ideal standoff distance is between 3 and 7mm, this distance is set by the calibration procedure within the “Set Z-height with Alignment Camera to Nozzle offset” sequence. Ensure that the nozzle will not collide with taller components on the substrate at the chosen offset distance • How do I shrink/expand my ink spot size? • To decrease your feature size, increase the sheath gas flow rate (S_MFC) to further focus the ink stream, to increase your feature size, decrease your sheath gas flow (S_MFC) • How do I increase my ink deposition rate? • Increasing the atomizer energy (UA_MAX) or increasing your atomizer flow rate (ATM_MFC) will increase your ink deposition rate • How can I speed up drying of my ink once it is printed? •

chunks.text: size, decrease your sheath gas flow (S_MFC) • How do I increase my ink deposition rate? • Increasing the atomizer energy (UA_MAX) or increasing your atomizer flow rate (ATM_MFC) will increase your ink deposition rate • How can I speed up drying of my ink once it is printed? • Increasing the platen temperature (PLATEN_HEAT) can help dry printed ink more rapidly and lock features in place to prevent ink blow-out • What is the idea number of passes for an aerosol jet print toolpath? • That depends a lot on your deposition rate, but it is best to start with a single test path to verify toolpath alignment and then print 2-4 passes to build up sufficient material. If the print is looking dry or discontinuous, continue to add more passes by running the toolpath again to build up material • What print and rapid speeds should I be operating the printer? • It is recommended to print at 2-3mm/s and use a rapid speed of 10 mm/s (which is the speed that the printer jogs between features). It should be noted that print speed also influences your deposition rate, the slower you move • How long will my ink stay stable and useable in the printer’s ink vial? • Aerosol jet printer inks are solvent based and will begin evaporating as soon as they are formulated, they are usually stable as long as solvent is being added back in the printing process but will dry out and become unprintable if the ink is left unattended. The printer should be cleaned at the end of each print session and new ink should be loaded the next time the printer is used • What solvent should I use in the solvent addback system? • The solvent in the add-back system should match the solvent base for the ink being printed, for example, use deionized water for Novacentrix Metalon JS-A426 silver ink and acetone for Norland NEA 121 dielectric ink • How should I store aerosol jet print inks when not in use in the printer? • Follow manufacturer recommendations for

chunks.text: should match the solvent base for the ink being printed, for example, use deionized water for Novacentrix Metalon JS-A426 silver ink and acetone for Norland NEA 121 dielectric ink • How should I store aerosol jet print inks when not in use in the printer? • Follow manufacturer recommendations for storage and pay attention to expiration dates. Inks like Novacentrix Metalon JS-A426 are meant to be stored in a refrigerator at less than 5°C and inks like Norland NEA 121 should be stored in amber or opaque vials since it is UV-curable. • Is it possible to remove a printed trace once it has been printed? • Printed traces are liquid until they are cured/sintered so they can often be wiped away with the appropriate solvent and a lint-free swab. The longer the trace sits on the substrate the harder it will be to remove. Be sure to clean the area thoroughly before attempting to reprint the trace. • What happens if I hit a mechanical limit switch in the course of operating the printer? • Hitting a limit switch will pause all motion and throw an alarm within the KEWB software. Navigate to the “Alarms” button on the bottom right of window, click “Ack All Alarms” as many times as necessary to clear the flashing red alarm codes and then manually jog the printer back into the safe zone (move up in the “z” direction first and then towards the center of the platen using the “x” and “y” jog buttons • What happens if I fail my initial leak check? • Failing a leak check could be indicative of a few issues but will require you to remove the printer cartridge to diagnose. First, check all o-rings in the ink vial assembly to assure they are properly seated and not damaged, replace any o-rings that appear dry, cracked, discolored or caked in ink material. Next ensure that the cartridge is well-seated against the printer alignment pins and that latch is secured, finally check the tube connections between the ink tube, vial assembly and nozzle to ensure they are

Attempt another leak check once the printer is reassembled. • Can I print multiple ink materials on top of one another? • This is possible, but you must fully cure each printed layer before adding another material. Silver inks should be sintered with the laser sintering module or at the appropriate time and temperatures and dielectric inks should be heat cured or UV cured to ensure successive layers do not blead into one another. • What should I do with the printer once the session is complete? • Stop all process conditions using the “Shutdown UA Process” sequence, wait until the printer registers as “idle” and then disassemble. Clean all ink-contaminated components in a beaker of the base solvent, placing the beaker in a sonicator to ensure a deep clean. The longer the ink sits in the system the more likely it is to corrode internal components so clean promptly after each print session.

PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC9412835 PMID: 36015668 Abstract An aerosol jet printing (AJP) printing head built on top of precise motion systems can provide positioning deviation down to 3 μm, printing areas as large as 20 cm × 20 cm × 30 cm, and five-axis freedom of movement. Typical uses of AJP are 2D printing on complex or flexible substrates, primarily for applications in printed electronics. Nearly all commercially available AJP inks for 2D printing are designed and optimized to reach desired electronic properties. In this work, we explore AJP for the 3D printing of free-standing pillar arrays. We utilize aryl epoxy photopolymer as ink coupled with a cross-linking “on the fly” technique. Pillar structures 550 μm in height and with a diameter of 50 μm were 3D printed. Pillar structures were characterized via scanning electron microscopy, where the morphology, number of printed layers and side effects of the AJP technique were investigated. Satellite droplets and over-spray seem to be unavoidable for structures smaller than 70 μm. Nevertheless, reactive ion etching (RIE) as a post-processing step can mitigate AJP side effects. AJP-RIE together with photopolymer-based ink can be promising for the 3D printing of microstructures, offering fast and maskless manufacturing without wet chemistry development and heat treatment post-processing. Keywords: photopolymer, photoresin, aryl epoxy oligomers, aerosol jet printing, reactive ion etching, 3D structures, microfabrication 1. Introduction Aerosol Jet Printing—AJP In a period of almost two decades, AJP has been consistently utilized in the field of printed electronics and bio-applications [ 1 ]. In the 2000s, due to significant advances in hardware and software for motion systems technology, commercial AJP models such as the Aerosol Jet (Optomec Inc., Albuquerque, NM, USA) and the Nanojet systems (Integrated Deposition Solutions Inc.—IDS, Albuquerque, NM, USA) were released [ 2 ]. These AJP equipment can reach printing resolution down to a few micrometers regarding line width, offering advantages of fast prototyping and high-volume manufacturing [ 3 , 4 ], being a maskless technique and non-contact printing process [ 5 ], and along with it, one can directly convert CAD (Computer-Aided Design) diagrams to CAM (Computer-Aided Manufacturing) tool paths (motion system actuation commands). AJP is considered as a non-contact printing technique; nevertheless, some authors also classify AJP as the so-called Direct Write (DW) printing [ 6 ]. It became an essential tool when three-dimensional substrates are used, and printing resolution in the range of hundreds down to a few micrometers is needed. Figure 1 represents the speed and spatial printing resolution of popular printing techniques. Figure 1. Open in a new tab Printing speed and resolution of some popular printing techniques. (Adapted from Wu (2017) [ 7 ] with permission). Figure 1 presents printing techniques such as gravure, screen, inkjet, flexographic and aerosol, showing the flexibility of applying different substrates, ink formulation and ink composites at different process parameters [ 8 ]. They do not require the usage of harmful chemicals and do not produce material waste [ 9 ]. Specifically, regarding AJP, one can observe the versatility of this technique, where resolution can be tuned from 10 to hundreds of micrometers line width, as well as speed printing varying from 1.0 × 10 −2 up to 1.5 × 10 2 mm · s −1 .
