Similar experimental observations showing that a non-monotonic variation of the OS with an increase in the ShGF rate has been reported previously. Such non-monotonic variation of the OS with the ShGF rate can be justified given the fact that the OS consists of ink particles of various sizes and the fact that the ink particles of various sizes exhibit different spread with the ShGF rate (see Figure 8). Ref. [6] also shows that unlike the OS for smaller ShGF rates, the OS for larger ShGF rates is not predominantly composed of smaller ink particles. Our numerical results showing a progressive increase in the spread corresponding to larger sized particles with an increase in the ShGF rate (caused by this phenomena of droplets crossing the nozzle axis and the causing over collimation) and the fact that at large ShGF rates the spread corresponding to d = 10 µm becomes comparable to d = 1 µm (see Figure 8) help to justify this experimental observation as well. The spread shown in Figure 8 shows a very interesting trend for d = 1 µm. The spread is non-monotonic with respect to the ShGF rate (i.e., the spread first decreases, then increases, and then again decreases) at the printing substrate. Increase in ShGF rate narrows the width of the CGF (see Figure 4), which in turn would invariably lead to a lesser spread. This is exactly what is witnessed at the nozzle exit for all the particle sizes, except for very large particles (d = 10 µm). As the particles move from the nozzle exit to the printing substrate, they are no longer under the action of the ShGF and hence there is a tendency to follow the diverging streamlines (Figure 6 shows these diverging streamlines). Smaller the particles lesser are the inertia and hence larger is this tendency to follow the streamlines. A larger ShGF rate will lead to a larger focusing (or a more enhanced narrowing) of the CGF. A larger ShGF rate will lead to a larger focusing (or a more enhanced narrowing) of the CGF. Therefore, beyond the nozzle exit where there is no ShGF, the divergence of the streamlines would be larger. This is established in Figure 6. Consequently, a larger ShGF leads to two competing effects - first it leads to a larger collimation of the CGF (which establishes why at the nozzle exit one always witnesses a lowering in the spread with an increase in the ShGF rate) and second it causes a larger divergence of the streamlines beyond the nozzle exit. For d=1 µm, that is, particles of sizes that better follow the streamlines, the large collimation effect dominates at large and small ShGF rates (leading to a decrease in the spread with an increase in the ShGF rate), while the effect of increase in spread due to the divergence of the streamlines dominates at an intermediate ShGF rate (leading to an increase in the spread with an increase in the ShGF rate). This justifies this highly non-monotonic variation of the spread with respect to the ShGF rate for d = 1 µm. [30] used small enough aerosolized NP-laden drops that can ensure AJ printed lines that are only 500 nm thick). For such particles, this tendency to obey the streamlines beyond the nozzle exit will be even more pronounced. Consequently, chances are that at the printing substrate this increase in the spread with an increase in the ShGF rate will persist over a much larger range of ShGF rates. 3.4. In the presence of a velocity gradient of the background flow at the location of an ink particle and the condition that the particle velocity is smaller than the background flow (these two conditions are always true for the present case), the Saffman effect would ensure that the ink particles experience a force that drive them toward the location of higher flow velocity, that is, in a radially inward direction for a Hagen-Poiseuille flow. As pointed out by Akhatov et al., the consideration of a Saffman lift force becomes important when the ratio, εF (see below) becomes significant (i.e., comparable to unity): εF = Fsa / Fst ~ 0.68d √(ρQtotal / (μDw³)) First, it can be easily understood from Equation (12) that the ratio εF dictating the impact of the Saffman force is much weaker for smaller sized particles (since εF ≈ d). A weaker Saffman force would imply a weaker collimation toward the nozzle centerline, and consequently the smaller ink particles would experience a much larger spread at both the nozzle exit and the printing surface. In addition, when the droplet size is very small, the Stokes force can generate huge acceleration on the droplet [since Fst ≈ 4.5πμ(u-up)d], while the Saffman force effect is negligible. Therefore, smaller particles speed up faster and tends to follow the fluid transport, so that the droplets with d = 1 µm travel from the nozzle to the substrate with the expansion of the flow. This supports the first observation of droplet size effect on collimation in the previous subsection, as well as different experimental results on AJP, namely the predominance of smaller-sized particles in the OS region particularly for low ShGF rates. This is especially evident in the spread of smaller particles, which tend to follow the fluid flow, and agrees well with the previous analysis in section 2.2 that indicates an increase in CGF focusing by increasing the ShGF rate (see Figure 4 and Eq. This observation also justifies the experimental results (the printed features presented in the bottom panel of Figure 7) where, especially for ShGF rates QshG < 150 ccm, there appears to be a lowering of the OS with an increase in the ShGF rate. The most challenging part of the explanation is to 1) justify the final observation as to why the OS first decreases (as described above), but then again increases with an increase in ShGF rate and 2) justify the reason for the lack of smaller particles in the OS region at larger ShGF rates. For these explanations, we resort to the analysis of Akhatov et al., who showed that when the ratio εF becomes significantly large, one witnesses an oscillatory behavior of particle trajectories, until the relative speed of the particle vanishes. Such an occurrence is due to the very weak relative damping effect of the Stokes drag force. This is exactly what happens when a very large ShGF rate is combined with large particle sizes, which results in a large value of εF. As a consequence, the larger sized particles will not encounter a damped motion and thus exhibit an oscillatory trajectory. It is because of such a trajectory that particles (with d = 10 µm) that start from the extreme opposite ends of the chamber cross each other [see Figure 7b-d, top] and impact the printing surface at locations that become more and more separated

This justifies why one witnesses an increase in the spread for the larger sized particles with an increase in ShGF rate, and hence justifies the experimental observation of an increase in the OS with an increase in the ShGF rate and a lack of smaller-sized particles in the OS region at larger ShGF rates. Finally, note that the channel size Dw also has an impact on εF, given that a smaller channel will increase the Saffman effect. Therefore, we suggest that if the AJP is operated with a smaller nozzle diameter and at higher gas flow rates, it would be desirable to have smaller diameter ink droplets with minimum polydispersity. Hereby, we conclude that there is a set of optimal parameters for good printing resolution, which includes the dimensions of the ink stream diameter within the nozzle, the size distribution of droplets within the ink stream and the CGF and ShGF rates. Further Discussions In sections 2 and 3, we study the OS formation in an ideal situation by carrying out our analytical and numerical study on the fluid dynamics and particle trajectories in perfect flow conduits, without considering the change in shape or size of droplets. However, these factors (e.g., post-impact change of the shape of the ink droplets or the geometric misalignment in the flow passage) will have a string bearing on the OS effect and will be important to explain phenomena such as asymmetric surface morphology of printed feature and droplet breakup at large ShGF rates. In this section, we identify two such factors that are rarely emphasized while probing the OS in an ideal setting: 1) velocity of the drops and their impact on the printing surface and 2) misalignment of the different parts of the nozzle. 4.1. Velocity Effects The ink particles impact the printing surface with a large velocity. The velocity variation (see Figure 9) after having exited the nozzle (Z = 0 mm) is highly intriguing, evidenced by the fact that, for particles of any size, the maximum velocity is attained at a location slightly below the nozzle exit. Also this maximum velocity is higher for smaller particles. That is, because there is a converging section of the nozzle from Z = 5 mm to Z = 0 mm, so that the flow velocity dramatically increases and smaller particles encounter a stronger acceleration due to the Stokes force. However, these smaller particles tend to follow the streamlines where they are located at the outer edge of the CGF, then expand outward from the centerline after exiting the nozzle and then quickly slow down due to the presence of the low velocity of

However, these smaller particles tend to follow the streamlines where they are located at the outer edge of the CGF, then expand outward from the centerline after exiting the nozzle and then quickly slow down due to the presence of the low velocity of the surrounding gas environment. Very interestingly, unlike the value of the maximum velocity, the velocity at the printing surface becomes non-monotonic with respect to the particle sizes for larger ShGF rates. Accordingly, the velocity at the printing surface first increases and then decreases with particle size. Larger particles are more centralized in the high velocity fields, and are imparted weaker acceleration by the Stokes force. This allows them to resist the change in velocity due to the disappearance of the ShGF more effectively. Of course, as is evident from Figure 9b, a decrease in the gap between the plate and the nozzle will keep the velocity at the printing surface monotonic, that is, the velocity at the printing surface would decrease with an increase in the particle radius. The most important consideration for this velocity variation is not the relative variation as a function of particle size but rather, it is the very magnitude of the velocity with which these drops impact the printing surface, in particular for larger ShGF rates. These velocities will imply an extremely large Weber number (We = ρp up² d/σp where ρp, up, and σp are the density, impact velocity, and the surface tension of the ink drops) which, for a significantly "philic” substrate, will lead to a significantly large deformation with a deformation ratio (which is the same as the spreading factor), that is, much larger than unity. Consequently, the drop will leave a large footprint on the printing surface, which may lead to OS in cases where 1) the deformed drop breaks and sticks to the surface without recoiling back, and/or 2) there is an in situ ultra-violet curing solidifying the drop at its deformed state, and/or 3) the drop splashes due to impact with such a large we number. To the best of our knowledge, such Weber number dependence of OS has never been probed and we plan to study that in great details in future work. 4.2. Misalignment Effect Misalignment of the CG flow direction with respect to the cylindrical axis of the ShGFannulus (resulting from issues related to the fabrication and/or assembly of the nozzle components or possible partial clogging of the flow passage due to the sticking of the ink particles on the inner walls of the flow passage), will break the symmetry of the ink stream flow and can be a major problem particularly for larger ShGF rates. In Figure 10a, we show such a misalignment (labeled as Δx) in the x-direction between the upper and lower solid components leading to asymmetry of the fluid conduit. We have carried out detailed simulations and have established that a misalignment as small as 0.1 mm in the design of the chamber or the nozzle of the AJ printer would lead to a notable distortion on the ink stream as it exits the nozzle, as is evident in the breakdown in symmetry of the trajectories of the ink particles of different sizes introduced into the chamber from opposite ends [compare the trajectories in 10(b) with those in 7c, upper panel]. As mentioned above, surface defects (e.g., some manufacturing defects or a stuck ink particle) can be a cause of this misalignment. Presence of such defects, as has been stated in section 2.1, is a key motivation as to why we consider the compressibility and turbulence despite the Reynolds number being in the laminar regime. It is worthwhile to note here that consideration of the possibility of turbulence (due to some possible defects) is a generic consideration without involving a specific case study demonstrating the exact scenario where a surface defect makes a laminar flow turbulent. Lack of such specific consideration also means that we are not in a position to exactly model the specific influence of the presence of the defects at various locations (e.g., at the nozzle exit) along the nozzle. However, we do make a qualitative statement on the role of such defects located close to the nozzle exit in such a situation, one would expect a massive effect on the printing resolution and given that the flow is unrestricted beyond the nozzle exit there is a possibility that the jet will be transformed into a spray. Here, we shall like to emphasize that we represent the misalignment effect as a simple geometric effect. Yes, as already mentioned, machining errors or stuck ink particles can cause such a misalignment; but, we only care about the geometric alteration in the flow passage due to this misalignment without caring for the specific flow physics associated with situations where the gas flow interacts with the surface defects like stuck ink particles. Therefore, a simple shift in the carrier gas flow along the nozzle chamber, as considered here, will indeed serve as an adequate representation of the problem given that we are interested in representing the misalignment effect as solely a geometric problem without caring much on what triggered (e.g., the presence of stuck ink particles) the misalignment. 5. Conclusions In this paper, we have carried out detailed numerical and analytical calculations to provide a rigorous analysis of the interplay between both the different gas flows and ink particles of different sizes primarily in terms of dictating the width of a printed line and the resulting OS phenomenon in AJP. We have limited our analysis to the flow-driven dynamics of ink droplets in determining the OS phenomenon assuming all droplets are gently deposited

We have limited our analysis to the flow-driven dynamics of ink droplets in determining the OS phenomenon assuming all droplets are gently deposited on the substrate. Our analysis has pointed to the vital role of the Saffman lift forces in ensuring a more collimated (hence narrower) line width for larger drop sizes, which explains the predominance of smaller-sized droplets in the OS region. Hereby, we conclude that there is a set of optimal parameters for good printing resolution which include the choice of nozzle exit diameter, size distribution of droplets within the aerosol, and the interplay between CGF and ShGF rates. Our findings, more importantly, illustrate an optimization problem of designing the aerosolization in a manner such that the carrier gas mainly consists of ink particles with sizes that simultaneously ensure a reduction in the OS and the ability to print features as small as tens of microns in dimension. Furthermore, we anticipate that our analysis will lead to a better understanding of the physics of the OS phenomenon, which in turn would empower us to address this optimization problem in more detail. chunks.text: Aerosol-Jet Printed Sensors for Environmental, Safety, and Health Monitoring: A Review ABSTRACT Aerosol-jet printing (AJP) is an emerging direct-write approach gaining attention for the rapid and affordable microadditively manufactured energy-efficient sensors and printed electronics. AJP accommodates a broad range of ink viscosities (0.001–1 Pa s) for printing diverse materials, including ceramics, metals, polymers, and biological matter. It produces reproducible, high-spatial-resolution features (approximately 10 µm) and allows for wide standoff distances (1–11 mm) between the nozzle and the substrate, facilitating conformal printing of complex geometrical designs on nonplanar, e.g., stepped or curved, surfaces. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of state-of-the-art AJP-based sensors, such as strain and temperature gauges, biosensors, photosensors, humidity and surface acoustic wave sensors, dielectric elastomer actuators, and motion, smoke, and hazardous gas detectors, and discusses prospective applications. The continuous effort to develop cost-effective, smaller, lighter, and better-performing devices remains a key challenge in printed electronics. Consequently, as AJP becomes increasingly utilized in the high-volume manufacturing of miniaturized active and passive sensors, it opens a pathway for facile, large-scale fabrication of devices for a wide range of consumer and industrial applications, including transportation, agriculture, infrastructure, aerospace, national defense, and healthcare. 1. Introduction The technology sector is constantly seeking innovative techniques for low-cost, high-throughput sensors and microelectronics. Printed electronics, in particular, show great potential for recyclable and biodegradable solutions, in addition to their other enabling benefits. The increasing proportion of electronic waste, with only about 25% estimated to be formally recycled, is a cause for alarm. Compared to traditional counterparts, printed electronics offer several benefits, such as minimization of energy consumption, attenuated use of hazardous substances, improved recyclability, and efficient use of materials for overall eco-designs. Within the printed electronics sector, direct-write methods are a leading approach to advanced manufacturing designs. While direct-write techniques were first developed to print conductive circuits using silver nanoparticle-based inks onto circuit boards, their use has grown in the scientific community to encompass a host of free-form deposition methods employing functional and structural ink formulations on flexible and rigid substrates. Compared to other direct-write additive manufacturing (AM) techniques, aerosol-jet printing (AJP) technology has expanded

Compared to other direct-write additive manufacturing (AM) techniques, aerosol-jet printing (AJP) technology has expanded beyond simple electronic circuitry to include actuators, sensors, and components used in active and passive wireless technologies and other microelectronic devices. The history of AJP as a 3D printing technique dates back to the late 1990s, when the government agency Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency-funded Mesoscale Integrated Conformal Electronics project aimed to develop manufacturing processes capable of depositing a range of materials onto virtually any substrate. Since then, AJP has emerged as an advanced manufacturing technique for the design and fabrication of diverse sensing modalities. Earlier studies often referred to AJP as M³D—Maskless Mesoscale Materials Deposition—as Optomec, Inc. originally commercialized the technology before adopting the Aerosol Jet trademark. The attributes of direct-write printing have generated ample interest for its increasing utilization in microelectronics fabrication across a highly diverse landscape of applications. For decades, microelectronic device fabrication relied on lithographic, screen printing, and other template-driven methods, which often require multistep deposition and an extensive toolset for subsequent removal of excess material. In contrast, direct-write AM techniques build 2D and 3D components layer-by-layer using computer-aided designs (CAD) without the need to generate patterned or physical masks. Maskless direct-write techniques such as AJP and inkjet printing (IJP) are economical, greener alternatives to conventional mask-based techniques because they use fewer resources and generate less hazardous waste, while enabling high-quality patterning not limited by a mask or template. Notably, maskless approaches are also better suited for rapid prototyping than traditional methods due to their ability to modify print patterns between runs without incurring costs or manufacturing delays associated with new mask production. AJP offers several distinct advantages to the field of microelectronic fabrication, summarized as "Greener," "Economical," "Throughput Miniaturization," "Customizable AM technique," "Diversity," and "Resolution" (including 10 µm spatial resolution). These advantages include the ability to accommodate a wide range of ink viscosities (i.e., 0.001–1

AJP offers several distinct advantages to the field of microelectronic fabrication, summarized as "Greener," "Economical," "Throughput Miniaturization," "Customizable AM technique," "Diversity," and "Resolution" (including 10 µm spatial resolution). These advantages include the ability to accommodate a wide range of ink viscosities (i.e., 0.001–1 Pa s) and to achieve high-spatial-resolution line widths down to approximately 10 µm through fine droplet production, making it a strong competitor against traditional approaches. AJP further enables printed sensors on diverse substrate materials, including polymers, ceramics, and silicon, as well as conformal printing on both stepped and curved surfaces. Accordingly, the market for integrating electronics onto and within objects, such as those achievable with AJP, is forecasted to grow significantly by 2032. Compared to conventional screen printing, which is an established technology, direct-write digital printing (like AJP) is an emerging technology bridging the gap between R&D and production. Screen printing requires contact-printing and screens, wastes expensive ink, produces thick layers (>10 µm) with low resolution (≈100 µm), has registration >25 µm, involves manual handling, prints on planar surfaces, uses high viscosity inks (0.1–60 Pa s), and creates very thick metallization layers, limiting spatial resolution and feature density. Direct-write digital printing, on the other hand, is contact-less and mask-less, uses efficient ink, produces thin layers (>1 µm) with moderate resolution (≈5 µm), has registration 5–20 µm, is automated, suitable for 2D and 3D substrates, uses low viscosity inks (0.001–1.0 Pa s), and allows for controlled thickness, multilayer, and multimaterial printing with low-temperature curing on flexible substrates like plastic, paper, and fabric. Comparing key properties, inkjet printing handles viscosities of 0.01–0.02 Pa s, line widths of 30–50 µm, and thicknesses of 0.01–1.0 µm, offering uniformity and application variety. Aerosol-jet printing handles viscosities of 0.001–1.0 Pa s, line widths of 10–120 µm, and thicknesses of 0.01–3.0 µm, known for high resolution and material variety. Screen printing handles viscosities of 0.5–5.0 Pa s, line widths of 30–50 µm, and thicknesses of 0.1–100 µm, characterized by particle load and high viscosity. Screen printing handles viscosities of 0.5–5.0 Pa s, line widths of 30–50 µm, and thicknesses of 0.1–100 µm, characterized by particle load and high viscosity. Advances in hardware manufacturing and design, spurred particularly by AM techniques, continuously drive consumers and industry to replace obsolete technologies with smaller, lighter, and better-performing devices. For optimal design and performance, sensors and other microelectronic components should be cost-effective, occupy minimal space, and conform to the device's shape and mechanical properties. The variety in AJP-based sensors drives applications into different niche markets based on academic and industrial interests. For example, directly printing conformal strain sensors onto flexible substrates or integrating them with embedded components enables new achievements in structural health monitoring (SHM) that offer a deeper understanding of mechanical stresses in infrastructure materials during manufacturing or under operational conditions. Likewise, biosensors (e.g., antibody detection platforms) and sensing modalities that monitor biologically and physiologically relevant processes (e.g., human activity monitors) utilize AJP's advantages for device miniaturization through printing biocompatible inks for wearable human performance monitors (HPMs) and cost-effective printed diagnostic assays. The development of AJP-based microelectronics fabrication for sensing and communication is also part of an evolution toward the Internet of Things (IoT) and Smart Connected Things (SCOT) for integration into networks of self-automated smart devices that respond to external stimuli and each other. Thus, as IoT and SCOT expand, AJP is applied to broader areas to ultimately drive sensor development and integration, with the potential to transform industrial solutions in the automotive, medical, aerospace, and energy sectors. Due to its ability for advanced manufacturing and additive integration of diverse materials, AJP reduces associated costs for IoT-based technologies by 20% compared to conventional methods. With the Fourth Industrial Revolution (Industry 4.0) underway, IoT-based sensors are not only the central driving force toward next-generation innovations but also encompass broader trends in smart technologies, including smart cities, smart homes, and smart factories. Despite widespread interest in AJP as a greener and more economical approach, no comprehensive review of AJP-fabricated sensors exists to date. Brief outlines in

Despite widespread interest in AJP as a greener and more economical approach, no comprehensive review of AJP-fabricated sensors exists to date. Brief outlines in broader reviews do not include recent progress, and other reports offer topical rather than comprehensive summaries. This paper provides an overview of the present state-of-the-art sensors achieved through AJP technology, along with future outlooks for these devices. 2. Working Principle The emergent AJP technique uses atomization and a stream of inert gas to deposit inks as focused aerosol sprays directed toward the printer platen within a wide standoff range (1–11 mm) between the nozzle and substrate. Longer standoff distances (i.e., 6–11 mm) can be realized by controlling atomization and gas flow parameters to print conformal patterns onto geometrically complex substrates. A typical AJP process involves two main steps: atomization and focusing. In atomization, a transducer generates atomized flow, creating ink concentration. In focusing, the aerosol flow passes through a print head, where a nozzle directs the sheath flow toward the substrate, maintaining a print speed and platen temperature. Either pneumatic (p-AJP) or ultrasonic (u-AJP; 1.6–2.4 MHz) atomization can be applied in the AJP process. Both modes can produce aerosolized print droplets in the range of 1–5 µm. However, there are notable operational differences. P-AJP supports high-viscosity inks (≈0.01–1 Pa s), but the aerosol spray's monodispersity is disrupted, resulting in inconsistent printed features. To obtain a narrow distribution of droplet sizes, a virtual impactor is required for removing droplets with insufficient inertia (<1 µm) or those exceeding the upper limit for fine printing (>5 µm), requiring larger ink volumes. U-AJP, despite a more restricted viscosity range (≈0.001–0.01 Pa s), produces uniform aerosol streams for more reproducible prints at a lower material cost. Operators must judiciously select deposition flow rates (atomization strength, aerosol gas flow rate, and sheath flow rate) to avoid scattering of weakly bound nanoparticles. To prevent system clogging, materials should not exceed 2 Pa s in viscosity or have

Operators must judiciously select deposition flow rates (atomization strength, aerosol gas flow rate, and sheath flow rate) to avoid scattering of weakly bound nanoparticles. To prevent system clogging, materials should not exceed 2 Pa s in viscosity or have an insufficiently large diameter (<500 nm recommended). Ink properties such as viscosity, surface tension, volatility, and density determine effective aerosolization and printing parameters. Following atomization, aerosol droplets are transferred to the deposition head in a plastic tube by a carrier gas flow, taking an average of 10 seconds to travel. During transport, some droplets collide with tube walls, preventing them from reaching the deposition head. Large and small droplets that do reach the deposition head are subject to gravitational settling and diffusion, respectively, affecting atomized ink output. Once at the deposition head, the focused stream is accelerated through a nozzle with an internal diameter of 50–300 µm and length of 20 mm. A stream of coaxial annular sheath gas flows through the print head to improve lateral resolution and increase velocity, enabling the focused deposition of a continuously flowing particle stream with velocities ranging from 10 to 100 m/s. Moving the building platform to CAD designs, layer contours can be printed with high resolution, and additional layers are deposited by sequential printing passes; thus, the aerosol stream remains uninterrupted during the process. Contemporary research harnesses the versatility of AJP to unlock challenging designs and complex material combinations in the sensor fabrication process with techniques for direct printing onto integrated circuits as well as in-situ monitoring for printing composite sensors or controlling the conductivity of traces without interrupting the printing process. The high print speed of AJP, coupled with its ability to support multiple printheads/modules, enables this technology as a viable candidate for the multilayered, multimaterial deposition of sensors and microelectronics. They must possess suitable rheological properties for effective aerosolization and printing. Ink parameters such as viscosity, surface tension, volatility, and density are critical for aerosolization and printing across different ink types. The "Z number," which combines viscosity, surface tension, and density, is an important dimensionless parameter for generalized ink formulations. In general, high boiling point/low vapor pressure solvents are employed in ink formulations and dispersed or solvated nanoparticles must fulfill several parameters: 300–500 nm maximum with <200 nm size preferred; solid content of 5–70% weight; and a shear thinning or Newtonian shear behavior. While most 3D printing specializes in a specific subset of ink classes (e.g., photopolymer), thermoplastics), AJP broadly accommodates inks formulated as a liquid ink (i.e., solvated or dispersed) and pneumatically or ultrasonically aerosolized, as theoretically comparable to commercial thermal evaporation methods. AJP-printed ink matrices include metallic, resistor, nonmetallic/conductive, dielectric/insulator, adhesive, resist, etching, and reactive chemistries-based formulations. AJP classically employs silver nanoparticle inks for its excellent line conductivity and low thermal degradation. Although unadulterated silver nanoparticles are a leading feature, other metallic nanoparticle systems such as silver nanowires (AgNWs) and silver-carbon composites including silver-palladium and silver-carbon nanotubes (CNTs) have been increasingly investigated. Due to their excellent electrical properties, other colloidal metallic nanoparticle systems have been employed, like gold nanoparticles and platinum nanoparticles. These latter options are less common in academic studies and industrial interests, perhaps due to higher material costs or challenges in manufacturing (e.g., synthesis of precursor inks, post-processing for annealing). While metallic inks are generally preferred for AJP, carbon-based nanoparticles, polymer-based inks, and ceramic-based systems are likewise emerging as alternatives. For instance, Ti3C2Tx MXene-based inks are gaining attention for their structural and physical properties, similar to graphene, but at a significantly reduced cost. MXene-based inks were first reported in 2019, and the influence of temperature on their resistance characteristics has been investigated. Biological ink formulations are also a mainstay of AJP sensing development, with research underway to optimize printing parameters for macromolecules (e.g., proteins, DNA). Inks with thermoelectric properties are also of interest for self-powered sensing devices. Recently, metal hydride-based materials (e.g., titanium hydrides (TiH₂)) have also been introduced as AJP inks. Despite their higher resistivity than silver- and copper-based nanoparticle inks, advantages of corrosion resistance, biocompatibility, improved stability, and versatility can be potentially unlocked for their integration to numerous applications. Carbon nanomaterials likewise remain a popular choice, as carbon inks, graphene, single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs), multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), sorted semiconductive derivatives, and metal composites thereof. While carbon nanomaterials alone may not confer the same electrical performances as metallic-based counterparts, they have several advantages when used as conductive reinforcements and fillers due to their large surface area and superior mechanical properties; notwithstanding, silver-CNT composite inks have been demonstrated to have considerably lower resistivities than pristine silver inks by functioning as bridges across granular boundaries and defects in the printed lines. Pure graphene inks, in particular, are highly promising materials toward printed sensor electrode designs owing to their flexible nature. Point defects within the crystal domain of the graphene lattice provide localized sites of high electrochemical activity for target analytes. Increasingly, polymer-based inks including conducting polyaniline, polymer pixels, solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs), and poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) have also been investigated using the AJP route as active sensing materials. A foremost consideration for stable polymeric-based inks is compatibility between the carrier solvent and respective polymer, based on the rule of solubility. Notably, polymer-based materials often have lower electrical conductivity than metallic counterparts and are more challenging to produce due to limited stability, solubility, and processability. Recently, new classes of functional materials—ionic liquids, ion gels, MXenes, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), transition metal dichalcogenides, and perovskites—have also been formulated as AJP inks, further underscoring the versatility of this technology and opening up an unexplored design space for printed sensing devices. In particular, due to their structural and physical property similarities to graphene, MXene inks have emerged as a valuable option at a significantly reduced cost. AJP compatible MXene inks were first reported in 2019, and the influence of temperature on the resistance characteristics of the printed patterns has recently been investigated. Biological ink formulations are likewise a mainstay feature of AJP sensing development, where the printing of macromolecules (e.g., proteins, DNA) is an active area of research with studies underway to optimize printing parameters. Also of interest are those inks with thermoelectric properties where thermal energy can be converted to electricity and vice versa, thus enabling a mechanism by which their integration can help to realize self-powered sensing devices. Accordingly, using AJP processes, several studies demonstrated maintained thermoelectric properties of such inks following the printing process. Substrates The substrate on which a pattern is printed functions as the base of the AJP sensor and may be attached to larger components or structures of interest. Alternatively, the materials of interest themselves may act as the substrate for an AJP sensor if an insulating layer is used to isolate the print from other conductive materials. In general, substrates support AJP designs, separate electronic devices from each other, and form the basis of the electronics package. Traditionally, the substrates of electronics are rigid and physically invariant. With advances in the field of printed electronics, the development of lighter, flexible, and biodegradable substrates has been realized. Key aspects when selecting substrates include their shape, intended application, thermal transmittance, mechanical properties, and sintering tolerance. Factors such as ink/substrate compatibility, interaction, adhesion, and wettability all play a role in the resultant print quality and performance of the fabricated device, and so it should be noted that the minimum feature size that AJP can achieve is substrate dependent. For example, features have been consistently printed at the lower resolution limit (≈10 µm) when employing SiO2 and polyimide (PI) substrates, which are often used in conventional microelectronics and chip fabrication. Moreover, printed patterns generally require a thermal curing step to remove organic solvents and additives used in the ink formulation as well as to sinter deposited ink into a dense and continuous pattern. Printing sensors directly on temperature-sensitive materials for some applications, including SHM (e.g., poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) conduit) or wearable HPMs (e.g., poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), polyurethane (PU), and cellulose-based materials) therefore requires alternative strategies to conventional thermal curing methods, as discussed in further detail in the following section. Although rigid glass and silicon substrates are classically employed for a wide range of AJP sensor modalities, flexible substrates including polymers (e.g., polyimide, PET, elastomers), cellulose-based materials and

Although rigid glass and silicon substrates are classically employed for a wide range of AJP sensor modalities, flexible substrates including polymers (e.g., polyimide, PET, elastomers), cellulose-based materials and even store-bought bandages are being progressively employed. For some flexible substrates (e.g., PET), the conformable morphology of these substrates coupled with the ancillary effect of transparency expands applications to future-forward ideas such as electronic skin and smart contact lenses. Moreover, composites of flexible polymers (i.e., polyimide) with classic rigid substrates (i.e., silicon or glass) have also emerged as hybrid systems that retain the properties of both materials. Sensor integration onto flexible substrates is ever-important for a variety of applications—wearables, portable electronics, healthcare devices, and other needs for our increasingly connected society. For the former—wearables—strips of textiles (i.e., fluorocarbon, nylon, and polymer fibers) have emerged as viable substrates. Outside of flexible designs, other interesting substrates have emerged such as direct prints onto PVC and acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS) pipings for direct monitoring of infrastructural strain and fatigue. With respect to SHM applications, authors have demonstrated prints onto carbon nanomaterial-based substrates including CNT networks and buckypaper. For direct integration onto printed circuit boards and other advanced technological devices, FR4 plastics and prepackaged integrated circuit platforms have been utilized. Considering other emerging sensing applications, fully freestanding functional devices have the potential to transform the landscape of wearable technologies and other application areas. Indeed, continued progression of AJP-based devices is expected toward continued miniaturization, increased flexibility, enhanced transparency, and designs that enable self-supported structures. 3.3. Thermal sintering of conductive metallic inks, the conventional selection for sensing electrode designs, is required for removing excess materials during sensor fabrication and ensuring the printed line is highly conductive

Thermal sintering of conductive metallic inks, the conventional selection for sensing electrode designs, is required for removing excess materials during sensor fabrication and ensuring the printed line is highly conductive and continuous. Following deposition, inks are cured and/or sintered based on substrate and material properties (≈110–300 °C for silver nanoparticle-based inks) with controlled profiles. Upon sintering, agglomerated metallic nanoparticles partially melt to form a cohesive solid, affecting electrical performance (resistivity, resistance) and mechanical performance (elastic modulus, shear strength). Lowering sintering time can decrease resistance by attenuating microcracks, while lowering sintering temperatures increases resistivity due to increased porosity. This thermal step is not an issue for metal or temperature-resistant polymer (i.e., polyimide) substrates, but it challenges materials with glass transition temperatures (Tg) or melting points (Tm) near or below the ink's required sintering temperature (e.g., ≈110–300 °C for silver nanoparticle-based inks). Exceeding the Tg or Tm of the substrate during thermal curing causes printed device deformation or degradation. To overcome these limitations, various low-temperature sintering techniques, including laser, light beam, xenon flash lamp, microwave, and electrical sintering, have been utilized. While these alternatives address substrate damage during postprocessing, they can be nontrivial to apply to complex 3D surfaces. Laser sintering is one of the most promising techniques due to its ability to maintain functionality in a 3D space, and several examples applying laser sintering to AJP-based sensors have been reported. As another strategy, low-temperature photonic sintering has been utilized. While laser and photonic curing avoid substrate damage, their throughput is unsuitable for roll-to-roll and large-area manufacturing. To combat this, pulse thermal processing (PTP), demonstrated in inkjet printing, may be used for low-thermal budget, industrially scalable integration of metal patterns onto polymeric, paper, and fabric substrates. PTP involves using a xenon flash lamp to deliver short-duration, high-intensity broadband light to generate high processing temperatures for thin film annealing, recrystallization, and compaction. 3.4. Characterization A variety of techniques are widely employed to characterize surface features, phase identification, and chemical properties (e.g., optical imaging, X-ray diffraction, photoelectron, and Raman spectroscopy) of AJP sensors. For graphene-based printed electrodes and sensing films, Raman spectroscopy (a nondestructive technique) is commonly used due to its high sensitivity for identifying different carbon structures and phases. For surface functionalization of graphene targeting C=O moieties as binding sites, surface-sensitive X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy is performed. For crystalline active materials, X-ray diffraction is used to confirm printed features' crystallinity. For atomic-level length scale materials (e.g., CNTs), microstructural properties of printed electrodes and thin films are explored via transmission electron microscopy or scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging, the latter often used with energy-dispersive X-ray analysis. Surface topography profiles and cross-sectional area of printed lines and film thicknesses are explored through atomic force microscopy. In addition to surface microstructure, both spatial resolution and line conductivity determine print quality. Electrical properties of AJP-based sintered printed lines are generally characterized through resistance measurements using two- or four-point probe methods. Parameters including carrier gas rate, stage speed, and focusing ratio affect resultant resistivity. In printed silver nanoparticle lines, calculated resistivity is approximately twice that of bulk silver, though some studies show equal conductivities. Particularly for wearable applications, fabricated devices require high stretchability and flexibility; therefore, characterizing mechanical properties of AJP-based sensors remains another key area of investigation. Within wearables, devices and interconnects must retain functionality under mechanical deformation, dictated by the underlying substrate's mechanical properties. Repetitive stretching or bending cycles are performed to elucidate how mechanical deformation affects subsequent performance, with some studies demonstrating structures that can withstand over 10,000 bending cycles with no loss of device performance. Both material type and intended sensing mechanisms/properties must be considered when selecting the most valuable characterization method. 4. Strain Sensors Strain gauge devices quantitatively transduce experienced strain or deformations into corresponding changes in resistance, capacitance, or piezoelectricity. Strain monitoring is essential in nondestructive mechanical testing for SHM, wearable HPMs, smart packaging, and human-machine interfaces. Conventional strain gauges typically consist of a sensitive grid (active layer), substrate, covering layer, and lead wire. When strain is applied, the grid's geometry distorts, changing its electrical resistance. The sensitive grid, which converts surface strain into relative resistance change, is often composed of thin alloy wire or foil traces (e.g., copper-nickel) laid in a meandering pattern, backed by a polyimide, epoxy, or fiberglass-reinforced epoxy substrate adhered with cements. Foil-based strain gauges are becoming obsolete due to their inconvenient size, rigidity, low operating temperatures, and failure under high strain rates. Maintaining strong adhesion between conventional strain gauges and structural materials is also a challenge. Direct-write methods are well-suited to replace conventional sensors as they enable functional material components (e.g., strain gauge patterns, insulating backing layers) to be directly printed onto the structural platform. Additionally, direct-write methods allow simpler fabrication, less toxic waste, and better optimal efficiency than conventional strain gauge fabrication, which typically involves mask transfer approaches like photolithography. The performance of strain sensors is quantitatively expressed as the gauge factor (GF), the ratio of relative change in electrical resistance to mechanical strain. AJP-based resistance-based strain gauges (RSGs) generally have higher GFs than conventional foil-based gauges, with some reports finding them capable of an order of magnitude larger GF values. Structural Health Monitoring AJP-enabled next-generation conformal microelectronics and SHM sensor designs integrated into IoT-based technologies can reduce downtime and repair costs through fast, location-specific detection of excess strain. Because AJP allows direct conformal prints onto objects, it offers greater insights into material performance and failure under operation. AJP has been widely investigated for integration into infrastructural materials. Early applications include a piezoresistive sensor based on metal-doped (m)-polyaniline in 2006, featuring a GF of 8 for pressure measurement on a sensing diaphragm. In 2010, Maiwald et al. reported an AJP-based RSG for nondestructive SHM, which outperformed reference foil-based counterparts (GF ≈3.35 vs ≈1.98). This design involved silver nanoparticle ink printed in a meander between polymer encapsulation layers on aluminum. Similarly, Zhao et al. fabricated strain sensors using silver nanoparticle-based inks directly printed onto carbon fiber prepreg, a lightweight structural composite, exhibiting a GF (≈2.2) comparable to commercial foil-based RSGs. These early examples showcased AJP's feasibility for fabricating embedded sensors to monitor mechanical properties and for complete lifecycle assessment of structural materials. Recent studies have examined commercial silver nanoparticle inks from NovaCentrix, designed for AJP with a PU adjuvant for improved substrate adhesion. Ratnayake et al. printed strain gauges on polyimide substrates and tested them on a cantilever beam, yielding comparable GFs of 1.74–1.85 to commercial metal foil-based gauges. AJP methods have also been used for temperature-sensitive curved material platforms, such as PVC conduits. Borghetti et al. reported printed RSGs on cylindrical PVC conduits and other plastics for SHM, using a composite ink of silver nanoparticles with a PU adjuvant, cured with a commercial photonic sintering instrument. These AJP sensors on PVC demonstrated an average GF of 2.42, comparable to commercial foil-based RSGs. Sensor-Enabled Smart Objects Smart objects with sensing components for acquiring and communicating information represent an evolving area. Direct printing of such components onto geometrically challenging objects is a cutting-edge development for digital transformation in various industrial applications, including healthcare, agriculture, and urban development. Ordinary objects can become smart by incorporating sensors, electronics, and network protocols, enabling data-informed decisions. Equipping objects with printed strain sensing capabilities has attracted significant interest. For instance, Borghetti et al. demonstrated a resistive sensing coil and tunable capacitor design using silver-based electrodes and polymer-based dielectric/insulating tracks to develop a passive telemetric system for measuring resistive loads. Such passive systems are viable for various industrial applications, e.g., smart packaging for the food industry, integrating multipurpose smart food tags (humidity, temperature, pressure, gas) for quality assurance and spoilage detection. While integrated sensors for smart objects are advancing, sensing strain on complex 3D shapes is challenging. Conventional RSGs are not ideal for 3D objects due to size, weight, rigidity, and planar surface attachment requirements, along with wired electronics. Recent advances highlight AJP's immense potential for conformally printing 2D microelectronics and wireless components onto structural parts with complex shapes while maintaining a small device footprint and lightweight design. Printing onto complex 3D shapes is enabled by AJP's wide standoff range (1–11 mm). By optimizing printing protocols and ink rheology, large z-direction changes during a single patterning run are achievable. Blumenthal et al. demonstrated that silver-based RSGs, electrical contacts pads, and wireless antennas could be printed on a carbon composite material with complex 3D shapes. Fujimoto et al. used AJP to equip soft structural textiles with flexible capacitive strain gauges (CSGs). Their investigations involved printing and sintering silver interdigitated electrodes (IDEs) on polyimide substrates, followed by drop-casting poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) as a dielectric material, and finally attaching the sensor to military-grade poly(p-phenylene terephthalamide) (Kevlar) with all-purpose barge cement. In static, dynamic, and cyclic tests, the printed CSGs outperformed commercial RSGs, with sensitivity values reaching GF ≈ 5.2 and capacitance values to 15 nF. Recently, the same research team also demonstrated a miniaturized Bluetooth-based wireless, multichannel readout system compatible with these CSGs for distributed monitoring of soft structural textiles in space applications. Changes in ambient temperature can affect strain sensor performance due to thermally induced modulations in printed traces' electrical properties. To address this, Rahman and others developed temperature-compensated strain gauge sensors to improve accuracy, as temperature-induced changes in sensing material resistivity can otherwise overestimate measurements. These sensors are useful in nuclear reactors and aerospace applications requiring exposure to extreme operating conditions. In parallel, space survivability of aerosol-printed materials has been explored. Ouchen et al. evaluated printed silver and gold test structures on ceramic and poly(tetrafluoroethylene)-based substrates in a NASA flight facility to test the effects of atomic oxygen, temperature cycling, and hard vacuum over six months. Their studies suggested that AJP-based structures can be used in space-based environments if a protective passivation layer is applied over printed metal traces. This achievement means AJP-based sensors resistant to space environments could be employed in integrated sensing platforms to monitor structural material degradation under atomic oxygen and ionizing radiation, similar to observations on on-orbit photovoltaic detectors. Studies are currently underway to discern the effects of gamma-ray radiation on aerosol-jet printed 2D materials (e.g., graphene, MoS2, WS2, BN) for space applications. 4.1.4. Human Health Monitoring Gathering precise human performance monitoring (HPM) data provides key insights into physiological information and biomedical metrics for human health, disease, and athletic performance. For telehealth and personalized medicine, integrating miniaturized sensors into wearable technologies is crucial. AJP, with its diverse substrate compatibility, is increasingly investigated for viable HPM-based devices. Combining AJP and photonic sintering has been applied to wearable strain sensors for healthcare on temperature-sensitive materials, including store-bought bandages. Agarwala et al. demonstrated direct patterning of silver nanoparticle inks onto bandage material, using a femtosecond-pulsed laser for localized heat to induce sintering with minimal energy transfer to the underlying substrate. AJP has also been applied to manufacture smart personal protective equipment (PPE). Given PPE's importance, Kim et al. explored AJP sensors for smart medical masks that monitor temperature and strain on the face of healthcare workers. An AJP silver strain sensor on polyimide was adhered to the mask's flexible portion near the nose bridge to wirelessly monitor healthcare professionals' temperature (irregular respiratory breathing, fever) and strain (face irritation, bruising). Recently, stretchable, soft material-enabled miniaturized strain sensors with tunable resistances and GFs (1–7.5) were demonstrated by Herbert et al. AJP was used to print polyimide and AgNWs for strain sensors that adhere to conformal surfaces without conventional fixtures, achieving reusability over ten times without loss of sensing performance for human motion and health. In another account, an orthogonally assembled hybrid silver nanorod/nanoparticle conductive network encased in poly(vinyl alcohol) detected human movement (e.g., joint bending, vocalization) with a reported GF of 23. Gas Sensors Monitoring specific gases (e.g., NO2, NH3, H2, CO2) as key indicators in domestic and industrial sectors is essential for preventing or reducing adverse effects on the environment and human health. Both 2D and 3D functional materials such as metal oxides, graphene, CNTs, conducting polymers, MOFs, and colloidal metallic nanoparticle systems have been custom-arily adopted as gas sensing materials. While metal oxide gas sensors are common, their fabrication typically requires complicated lithography or microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) processes, and they must operate at relatively high temperatures, requiring heaters. Other systems, like conducting polymers, can be manufactured using standard photolithography, but direct-write methods simplify advanced manufacturing processes for large-area arrays. Miniature gas sensors (lower weight, power consumption, affordable cost) are desired for real-time continuous monitoring with high temporal and spatial precision. Given the central focus on connected automation and IoT integration in Industry 4.0, printed gas sensing technologies, particularly AJP, have gained importance for fabricating microscale devices with these qualities. Applications include national defense, nature conservation, personal health monitoring, and smart cities, enabling lightweight, portable gas-detecting devices for tactical military operations, explosives and nerve gas detection, early detection of refrigerant gas leaks, and early warning systems in coal mining. Integrated Microheaters Considerable effort is directed at designing power-efficient microheaters for portable gas detectors, thermal actuators, microfluidics, and thermal metrology. Traditional hot-plates are ineffective for portability or remote operation, necessitating miniaturization to reduce power consumption and integrate with multiple sensing units. In metal-oxide semiconductor gas sensing, microheaters enhance target gas desorption and improve sensing performance. However, achieving low power consumption and high thermal uniformity remain main challenges. Optimized microheater designs are actively investigated for gas-sensing applications to provide low power operation while maintaining high sensitivity and stability. Manufacturing microheaters requires a delicate balance of geometrical, mechanical, thermal, and electrical specifications. Additive manufacturing approaches such as AJP are promising candidates for their fabrication. For example, Arsenov et al. demonstrated fully functional AJP-based platinum microheaters on ceramic substrates, exhibiting 640 mW power consumption at 225 °C. Khan et al. established a Pd-doped tin oxide (SnO2) sensor on polyimide substrates where gold transducer, microheater, and electrodes were printed using AJP for CO and NO₂ monitoring. This integrated resistive heater supported operating temperatures of 250–300 °C at low power consumption of 78–100 mW. A similar study used AJP to produce miniaturized gold microplates on flexible polyimide substrates with efficient power consumption of 54 mW at 325 °C. A parallel work included patterning gold-based microhotplates with ultralow power efficient heating (i.e., 12 °C mW⁻¹) on double meander 150 × 150 µm² heaters. Relative Humidity Monitoring relative humidity (RH) is highly crucial for environmental control, especially when integrated with other sensors (e.g., temperature) in settings like hospitals, pharmacies, manufacturing centers, residential and commercial buildings, food processing industries, and agriculture. Humidity monitoring improves human health and comfort, contributes to food safety, reduces waste, and enhances plant health. Integrating AJP into 3D structures offers a path toward customizable application-specific integrated circuits that are compact, low-cost, flexible, and biodegradable. Paper substrates are gaining attention for printing electronic devices. A low-cost capacitive-type RH sensor with printed interdigitated architecture on paper was fabricated for critical infrastructure health monitoring, showing ability to measure humidities in the range of 20% to 90% RH. Hysteresis effects are more significant on moisture-sensitive substrates, requiring careful attention to fundamental reaction mechanisms for performance optimization. High metal-line conductivities on cellulose-based substrates remain challenging due to ink bleeding, surface roughness, and general incompatibilities with sintering processes. Oxidants and Reductants Sensors capable of monitoring toxic reducing and oxidizing gases (e.g., NO2 and H2O2) are needed in various industrial and environmental conditions. NO2 is a regulated toxic pollutant, requiring routine monitoring by governmental agencies. NO2 sensors monitor vehicle exhausts, off-gases from fossil fuel combustion, pesticide-laced agricultural runoff, industrial effluent, smog buildup, and acid rain precipitates. Carbon-based nanomaterials show promise for NO2 monitoring. Zhou et al. printed chirality-sorted semiconducting SWCNTs as thin-film transistors onto HfO2-coated silicon substrates, achieving NO2 detection down to 60 ppm with enhanced selectivity. Following a similar approach, Kubersky et al. manufactured an ethylene gas sensor to reduce fruit and vegetable waste during storage and transportation, with sensitivity down to 0.14 nA ppm⁻¹. AJP was used to deposit gold working electrodes on ceramic substrates for this sensor. Flammables AJP's versatility has been demonstrated for developing flammable gas sensing technologies, including hydrogen (H₂), hydrogen sulfide (H2S), and ammonia (NH3) detectors. Due to H₂'s heavy industrial use, reliable sensors are vital for operational safety and minimizing environmental concerns. H₂ is a promising alternative energy source, but its fast flame propagation velocity causes explosions at concentrations as low as 4% by volume in air, making early leak detection crucial. SWCNT-based H₂ sensors decorated with metal nanoparticles (e.g., Pt, Pd, Au, Ag) promise increased sensitivity, lower detection limits, and faster response/recovery times over traditional metal oxide counterparts. Liu et al. reported an H₂ sensor based on Pt-decorated SWCNTs on silicon substrates, fabricated by AJP. Pt nanoparticles adhered to CNTs catalyzed H₂ dissociation, converting Pt into platinum hydride (PtHx), which bridges electron transfer to the CNT layer, changing its electrical properties. Through AJP's nanoparticle-sized droplets, Liu et al. showed suppression of the "coffee ring effect" (dispersed SWCNTs aggregating toward substrate edges due to capillary flow) and achieved a low H₂ detection limit of 20 ppm with a uniform network of homogeneously dispersed Pt-decorated nanotubes. Biosensing and Healthcare Applications Reliable, disposable, user-friendly biosensors fabricated with facile manufacturing methods are in high demand for monitoring disease progression, protecting human health and safety, and fighting pandemics. Biological sensors transform chemical information from analytes' concentrations into an electrical or other analytical signal. Three main thrusts for biosensor development are biocatalytic (enzyme), immunological (antibodies), and nucleic acid (DNA). Biosensors consist of four fundamental components: a sensing element/receptor, an interface for the biological elements, a transducer for physical/chemical information to analytical signals, and electronic equipment for signal processing, amplification, and interface. Traditional biosensor fabrication, using screen printing electrodes, limits device size. Thus, AJP has been applied to miniaturize devices capable of continuous real-time monitoring of biological phenomena. AJP's biological applications date back to the early 2000s when Optomec filed a patent for aerosolized delivery of bioinks. Since then, AJP's use in biologically relevant approaches has risen significantly and become an active area of sensor development. The diversity of materials required for biosensor fabrication reflects the diversity of the human body. Common active components under AJP processes include metallic nanoparticles (silver, gold, metal oxides), carbon nanomaterials (SWCNTs, MWCNTs, graphene), and conducting polymers. Bioinks For biomolecule printing, controlling the position of living cells on a substrate is important for biosensor fabrication and studying cellular interactions. Early work in the 2000s by Optomec researchers aimed to direct-write biological materials at mesoscale resolution (10 µm to several millimeters) to position mammalian 3T3 mouse fibroblast cells on Petri dishes, noting proliferative growth after 72 h incubation. Another study used adhesive bioactive and nonadhesive (hydrophobic) bioinert polymers to create positively and negatively patterned regions on glass for cell adhesion or exclusion. Shortly after, Große Holthaus and Rezwan demonstrated printing a bioceramic (calcium phosphate) as a substrate for bone growth studies. AJP successfully constructed bioceramic surfaces enabling cell proliferation, but slow processing times and system variability were noted. Early studies suggested that printing with an ultrasonic unit could damage active enzymes and DNA due to shear forces, recommending pneumatic aerosol formation for biomolecules. However, a more recent study challenged this, revealing protein reagents incurred no damage with ultrasonic units, achieving highly sensitive immunoassays for biological reagents printed on polymer brushes. Since u-AJP uses considerably less material than p-AJP, retaining biofunctionality in bioinks comparable to IJP promises cost-effective in vitro diagnostic assays. Another recent study systematically investigated critical printing parameters for bioink delivery via u-AJP, successfully achieving gelatin line widths down to 20 µm as a model bioink. In recent years, printing pure collagen matrices (without gelatin or alginate adjuvants) has also been explored. Gibney and Ferraris demonstrated bioprinting collagen types I and II via AJP to replicate dense collagenous matter in extracellular matrices of connective tissues. Mimicking complex microenvironments similar to extracellular matrices is challenging, requiring rapid screening of biomaterials with high-resolution design flexibility (iterative patterning). AJP has been explored as an enabling bioprinting process. For instance, Capel et al. investigated AJP for depositing controlled microscale PEDOT:PSS patterns to create neuronal culture environments on glass and PKSPMA-coated glass platforms. These biointerfaces promote cell attachment for up to 96 h without degradation, demonstrating AJP's value in bioprinting for organized networks of cell guidance designs in in vitro cell culture studies. Such digitally driven designs extend the diversity of studies achievable across different biological environments. 4.3.2. AJP's tissue engineering applications date back to 2006, when Liu and Webster demonstrated scaffolds of poly(lactide-co-glycolide) with dispersed titania nanoparticles for orthopedic tissue engineering. After seeding with human osteoblast cells, authors observed enhanced osteoconductivity and accelerated cellular growth, suggesting the nanocomposite mimicked natural bone properties. For myocardial infarction, Basara et al. mimicked cardiac tissue's extracellular matrix and electroconductivity by printing a conductive MXene structure on predesigned poly(ethylene glycol) hydrogels using AJP at cellular resolution. The engineered composite provided topographical and conductive cues for stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes to form cardiac patches for myocardial infarction injury. MXenes offer cytocompatibility for conductive biomaterials, and with AJP's conformal printing advantages, fabricated hybrid tissue constructs are promising as electroconductive scaffolds for cardiac patches. In addition to cardiac repair, other studies used blended inks of conducting polymers (PEDOT:PSS) and MWCNTs to print (via combined IJP and AJP processes) 3D microelectrode arrays (needle-like tips with 10 µm diameter, 33 µm height) that responded to extracellular signals from cardiomyocyte-like HL-1 cells, further endorsing AJP's feasibility for exploring and understanding cellular electrophysiological properties. Tonello et al. assembled a low-cost impedance-based approach to monitor cell proliferation of human mesenchymal stromal cells using carbon inks AJP deposited onto flexible polyimide substrates. Impedance variations were compared against enzymatic proliferation assays for a noninvasive approach to monitoring scaffold culture systems. 4.3.3. Following this approach, Martin et al. recently reported printed DEAs as a functional iris implant allowing focus adjustments for surrounding light conditions. Additionally, actuators designed similarly, based on stacked medical grade silicones for applications in healthcare, have been demonstrated. EMG and EKG Electromyogram and Electrocardiogram (EMG/EKG) EMG and EKG electrodes have been recently explored via AJP. Printed bioelectronics address common medical diagnostics and manufacturing challenges typical with conventional electrodes. In many clinical setups, electrodes must have low impedance at the skin/device interface, with conformable designs that fit curved body surfaces. Initial research demonstrated that direct-write printing provides robust devices, offering benefits of direct-write printing such as compatibility with flexible substrates, lightweight, and user-friendly electrodes. Kwun et al.'s investigations demonstrated a combination of silver nanoparticle and graphene inks onto elastomeric substrates to print EMG/EKG sensors. Printed directly on the skin, these conductive films showed excellent biocompatibility. Compared to commercial devices, the fabricated sensors displayed acceptable levels of signal-to-noise ratio and motion artifact reduction. Six different muscle activities were monitored using EMG sensors, demonstrating AJP's feasibility for real-time monitoring of EMG signals in external machines, such as robotic arms and hands. Accordingly, in a recent study, a noninvasive multisensing platform for muscle fatigue in rehabilitation was explored using printed biosensors. Physical fatigue measurements in lactate and biochemical activities were quantified. Biorecognition The recognition of biological molecules at ultralow concentrations is urgently needed for diagnosing and monitoring human disease. AJP has been recently explored as a technique for constructing sensitive and selective biosensors that detect antibodies, antigens, and neurotransmitters. An ultrasensitive phenylethyl boronic acid-functionalized rGO field-effect transistor was fabricated by AJP on PET for rapid and real-time detection of specific biomolecules. An immunosensor for rapid monitoring of interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin 10 (IL-10) cytokines was demonstrated by printing a graphene-nitrocellulose ink onto polyimide substrates in an IDE pattern. The fabricated devices were highly selective, monitored a wide sensing range (e.g., 0.1–5 ng mL⁻¹ IFN-γ), demonstrated a rapid response time (33 min), and exhibited low cross-reactivity with other antibodies (e.g., IL-6). Diagnostics AJP has been applied for diagnostic usage across various medical conditions—diabetes, wound care, blood diseases, and portable drug testing kits. As healthcare costs rise, early diagnosis improves recovery and lowers treatment costs. Rapid advancements in printing technology and materials enable additively manufactured biosensors to expand medical diagnostics. Monitoring glucose in the clinically relevant range (3–10 mM) is important for early diabetes detection and cellular process monitoring. Yang et al. designed a dual glucose/H2O2 sensor using a silver microelectrode array for catalytic reactions. Glucose oxidase, as a model enzyme, catalyzes glucose oxidation to H2O2, achieving high sensitivity (LoD, glucose = 1.7 mM). For noninvasive diabetes diagnosis, a semiconductor-based gas sensor was microadditively manufactured using SnO2 thin films for acetone vapor detection via breath analysis. Organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) have also been employed for glucose detection. AJP simplifies manufacturing processes by printing OECTs via four varying functionalizations: unfunctionalized device/GOx; PEDOT:PSS/GOx; printed Pt gate/GOx; and sputtered Pt gate/GOx. Another interesting application of AJP-based OECTs for biosensing is the creation of rapid, portable drug testing kits. Following legalization efforts, reliable detection of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC) remains elusive for law enforcement and healthcare. Portable saliva kits that detect Δ9-THC are of growing interest due to ease of accurate detection. Majak et al. utilized AJP to design an unfunctionalized OECT, noted for its ability to function well in aqueous media, with printed PEDOT:PSS as the channel material and printed silver nanoparticles for both source and drain electrodes on polyimide substrates. Microfluidics In parallel with biotechnological applications, integrating biosensors with microfluidics can revolutionize biological and biomedical research. Early microfluidics chips were produced from silicon under clean room conditions using expensive photolithography. Now, fine chip structures, chambers, and channels can be produced more economically without additional assembly steps due to advances in direct-write printing technologies. AJP has the potential to transform microfluidic device fabrication with customized geometries and added functionalities rapidly and at reduced material cost. Novo et al. designed and fabricated an electrochemical microfluidic sensing platform entirely printed by AJP for standard enzyme-mediated glucose monitoring, with results showing sensing capability in a clinically relevant range of 3–10 mM. Catic et al. demonstrated AJP's feasibility for rapid production of microfluidic molds. Another approach toward manufacturing microfluidics includes roll-to-roll hot embossing of microfluidic channels where AJP gold nanoparticles were used to manufacture high-throughput, highly efficient, and homogenous surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) structures. This study demonstrated AJP-modified fabrication of microfluid SERS chips for quantitative analysis of chemicals and biomolecules. 4.4. As a fundamental building block for light-based systems, photosensors find applications in wearable health monitors, medical imaging, digital logic, RFID tags, ambient light sensors, among others. Over past decades, photosensors have been developed for a wide range of wavelengths (infrared, visible, ultraviolet), increasing their role in sensing. Visible light detectors are traditionally employed, but growth in IR- and UV-based technologies has expanded applications in civil and military defense, environmental, and biological imaging. Coupled with direct-write printing advantages, photosensors can be used as large-area arrays and disposable paper-based modalities. Increasingly, AJP has been applied to fabrication to produce devices with next-generational aims using diversified advanced materials as inks and substrates. Traditionally, crystalline inorganic semiconductors are used as the sensing layer in photosensors. While these materials have advantages (e.g., Si-based photosensors integrate with underlying circuitry), they suffer from costly, high-temperature lithography-based fabrication processes that require rigid, thick active layers, precluding flexible substrates. Alternative photosensor materials (perovskites, organic semiconductors, colloidal quantum dots), amenable to aerosol-jet printing, have attracted interest for their ability to scale into large-area arrays on flexible substrates. Photosensor performance is typically measured via metrics like noise, speed, and efficiency; photoresponse strength is termed as responsivity (ampere/watt (A W⁻¹)). While AJP-based devices' performance is comparable or even higher than state-of-the-art, more research is needed to understand how fundamentally defect-free films and optimal performing photodevices can be unlocked using AJP. Photodetectors The first AJP-based organic photodetector was developed by Wang et al. in 2013, involving metalloporphyrin-based nanowire networks of zinc with light-harvesting properties printed onto PET substrates. The prototype demonstrated high photosensitivity, fast response, and recovery times, associated with the large surface-to-volume ratio of nanowires, which facilitates efficient surface-dominated oxygen chemisorption/desorption. Aga et al. used a combination of AJP, inkjet printing, and drop-casting to produce a low-cost polymeric photodetector on paper. Authors designed these flexible photodetectors by inkjet-printing a silver electrode onto photo paper, followed by AJP deposition of conductive PEDOT:PSS as a subsequent interlayer and top electrode, with an AJP photoactive layer of poly(3-hexylthiophene):C61-butyric acid methyl ester blend (P3HT:PCBM) followed by a drop-casted highly transparent and conductive deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) biopolymer layer. The printed photodetector exhibited a photoresponse in the visible spectrum with two orders of magnitude lower responsivity than commercial Si counterparts. Nevertheless, integrating these printed devices onto paper substrates opens a route for designing inexpensive, disposable optical sensors. Aga et al. also studied PEDOT:PSS thickness on oxygen plasma-treated Ni electrode for work function modification, demonstrating a threefold increase in photoresponse of a polymer-based (P3HT:PCBM) Schottky barrier photodetector compared to devices without PEDOT:PSS coatings. AJP technology has also been employed in dichalcogenide-based (e.g., WSe2, MoS2) photodetectors. For instance, a fully printed CNT/WSe2 photosensor on flexible polyimide substrates was demonstrated, where transparent CNT electrodes enabled incident light passage through the CNT/WSe2 heterojunction for photocurrent generation. Results showed comparable photoresponsivity in the visible spectrum compared to other flexible photosensors. Photodiodes Early work in AJP-based photodiodes by Eckstein et al. demonstrated the fabrication of inverted configuration semiconductor (transparency < 15%) organic photodiodes (OPDs) in the visible. Substrates utilized were conformally printed flexible organic photodetectors based on a blend of poly(thienylene)-co-benzodithiophene (PTB7) and [6,6]-phenyl-C71-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM) as the light-absorbing layer. The performance of the fabricated semitransparent photodetectors was found to be equivalent to state-of-the-art devices constructed on rigid substrates and outperformed previously reported all-printed OPDs without the use of other sophisticated fabrication processes (e.g., spin-coating, sputtering). Eckstein et al. further developed an OPD array (active area 250 µm × 300 µm) to produce 1D photosensor arrays, with 256 OPD pixels with high spectral responsivities (0.3 A W⁻¹) and specific detectivities (>10⁹ Jones), comparable to state-of-the-art inorganic photodiodes. Near non-fullerene acceptors, namely, IDTBR:P3HT, have been explored by Strobel et al. toward developing high performance OPDs with spectral tunability. These novel materials achieve responsivities in the WE and near-IR, and devices outperform detection needs of fullerene-based systems. AJP offers solutions to challenges in organic material extraction, such as bulk heterojunction bleeding and optimal electron-hole extraction. By designing a bulk heterojunction scheme, the authors create a donor P3HT bulk heterojunction without the need for orthotropic gradients, which enables optimal electron and hole extraction and noise reduction. 4.4.3. While LEDs are most commonly used in digital displays or as broadband light sources, they are also utilized in photosensors for diverse applications such as bidirectional communications and ambient light level sensors. Therefore, AJP's application toward LED manufacturing represents an emerging area of investigation for potential sensor integration.
